articles.title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
articles.body:
A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.
Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.
Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.
Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.
“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.
Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.
“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”
Weaponization
The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.
Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.
Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.
Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.
Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.
Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”
‘False’ allegations
Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.
On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.
Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”
The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”
During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.
Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.
In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.
A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.
That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.
Trust exercise
Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.
The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.
The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.
Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.
A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”
Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.
That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.
“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”
Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

Statements by Pyotr Tolstoy, deputy speaker of the Russian State Duma, regarding strikes on Ukrainian urban centers amount to public calls for war crimes, according to Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.

articles.title: Greece, Israel to ink deal for air defense systems
articles.body:
Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion air defense agreement with Israel in Tel Aviv on Aug. 31, in what will become the largest defense export deal in Israeli history.
Negotiated over the past three years, the agreement will give Greece its first integrated, multilayered air defense network, designed to counter a range of potential threats, especially from Türkiye, according to the Greek media reports.
A Greek delegation will sign the deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to acquire systems from Israeli defense companies Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI).
Rafael will supply David’s Sling systems, capable of intercepting heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles. IAI will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.
The deal will also include a national command-and-control center, modeled on Israel’s system, to coordinate the air defense network and manage launches. The center will incorporate artificial intelligence capabilities.
Known in Greece as the “Achilles Shield,” the project is expected to cost around 3.1 billion euros.
Greek officials said outstanding issues were resolved in recent days, including a requirement for 25 percent Greek participation in the project and the transfer of source code.
Twelve Greek companies are expected to participate as subcontractors to Rafael and IAI, undertaking more than 700 million euros worth of work.
The agreement comes as Greece, Greek Cyprus and Israel have stepped up security cooperation in recent years amid heightened tensions with Türkiye. Greek Cyprus has also reportedly acquired Israel’s Barak MX system to bolster its air defenses.
The previous largest Israeli defense export deal was IAI’s $3.5 billion sale of the Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany, signed in 2023.

Ukrainian USF destroy five Russian air defense assets at Yeysk and Millerovo airfields
According to Ukrinform, Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, reported this on Facebook.
According to Brovdi, during the August 30 operation against Russian military airfields, drones operated by the “Birds” of the First Separate Center struck a Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft missile and gun system, a Sopka-2 (12L6) radar station and an aviation weapons depot in Yeysk, Krasnodar Krai.
In Shabelskoye, Krasnodar Krai, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Kasta 2E2 radar station.
At the Millerovo airfield, located near the settlement of Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov region, ammunition depots and a technical and maintenance unit were destroyed.
The forces also struck an RSP-27 (DRL-27) radar and a Nebo-SV radar in Dolotinka.
According to Madyar, the main target of the operation was the DRL-27 module of the RSP-27 aircraft landing radar system at the Millerovo airfield. The destroyed DRL-27 is an airfield control radar that, in addition to detecting airborne targets, is an integral component of air traffic control and operates as part of a system with the PRL-27 landing radar.
“The destruction of the above-mentioned enemy air defense assets has been confirmed by additional reconnaissance,” the USF commander said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s Defense Forces previously struck a Russian radar station, command posts and a Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft missile and gun system.

articles.title: Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
articles.body:
Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
The mutiny began at a military base in Niamey and spread near the presidential palace and state broadcaster.
In the latest turmoil to hit Niger in West Africa, the military-led government says it has contained a mutiny in the capital, Niamey, after hours of gunfire and explosions near key military and government sites.
A military base at Diori Hamani International Airport was first targeted on Saturday by renegade soldiers, followed by attacks on the state broadcaster and presidential palace.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Niger military says it is regaining control after attempted mutiny
- list 2 of 3Gunfire, blasts in Niamey as soldiers mutiny in Niger’s capital
- list 3 of 3Tuareg rebels free more Malian soldiers in prisoner swap, sources say
State TV said security forces gradually regained control, while dozens of rebel soldiers were reportedly killed or arrested.
The mutiny is another blow to Niger’s military leadership, which has failed to bring stability to the country since it took over in a coup three years ago. Since then, the military ruler and President General Abdourahamane Tchiani has pivoted the country away from the West, including its former colonial ruler, France.
He has forged close security ties with Russia in efforts to tackle the growing threat from armed groups, but that has not deterred fighters linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) from mounting attacks.
So what happened, who was behind the mutiny and what does it mean for Niger’s military government?
What happened?
The attacks started shortly after midnight on Saturday at Base 101, a major military facility inside Niamey’s international airport complex previously used by US forces.
General Salifou Mody, Niger’s defence minister, said a group of soldiers detained some of their comrades and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the capital.
The fighting lasted for several hours, during which the state broadcaster was temporarily taken off air, while gunfire and explosions were reported around the airport and presidential palace.
Authorities said security forces responded quickly and helped regain control. The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, urged people to remain calm.
“Our Defence and Security Forces are mobilised for the Defence of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive,” it said.
By late Saturday, military authorities and state TV said the mutiny had been contained. Dozens of soldiers had been killed or arrested. Africa Corps, the Kremlin-backed force, received a request for assistance in neutralising the mutineers in the capital, said Viktor Voropaev, the Russian ambassador to Niger, in an interview with TASS news agency on Saturday.
Africa Corps is a Russian state-controlled paramilitary organisation established by the Russian Ministry of Defence, replacing and absorbing the African operations of the privately -run Russian militia, the Wagner Group.
The whereabouts of military leader Tchiani have not been confirmed.
Base 101 houses the general staff of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), which includes Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. The AES was established in 2023 to combat armed rebellion in the Sahel region.
It also houses the headquarters of the Africa Corps, which supports Sahel states in combating armed groups.
Who were the renegade soldiers behind the mutiny?
The mutineers appear to have included young soldiers from areas outside Niamey, particularly the southwest of Niger.
Reuters news agency reported that the operation involved soldiers from Ouallam, Tera and Dosso, citing analysts and security officials. Troops from those areas have suffered heavy losses fighting armed groups, particularly the regional ISIL affiliate.
The exact size of the mutinous force, and who led the mutiny, was not immediately clear. But analysts said the involvement of frontline troops points to growing frustration within the military.
“These mass-casualty overrun attacks on the Nigerien military are becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks,” said Heni Nsaibia, senior West Africa analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED).
Timeline of unrest in Niger
July 2023 – Niger’s military government seized power in a coup, saying the elected government had failed to contain armed groups.
August 2023: Regional bloc ECOWAS imposes sanctions and threatens military intervention; Tchiani proposes a three-year transition.
September 2023: Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso establish the Alliance of Sahel States (AES). France agrees to withdraw its ambassador and 1,500 troops.
January 2024: Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso announce their withdrawal from ECOWAS.
June 2024: An attack in western Niger kills 20 soldiers and a civilian, one of the deadliest assaults on the military since the coup.
September 2024: Niger suspends its military pact with the US. Washington subsequently withdraws its troops and closes its two bases – Air Base 101 in Niamey and Air Base 201 near the northern city of Agadez. Built at a cost of more than $100m, Air Base 201 was used for manned and drone surveillance flights and other operations in efforts to target ISIL fighters and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a regional affiliate of al-Qaeda.
October 2025: Kevin Rideout, a pilot with the evangelical missionary agency SIM International, was abducted in Niamey.
January 2026: ISIL claims responsibility for an attack on an air force base at Niger’s Diori Hamani International Airport and the adjoining military base in Niamey.
June 2026: An armed attack on Niamey airport kills 11 soldiers and two civilians.
August 29, 2026: Soldiers mutiny at Niamey’s Base 101, with gunfire around the airport, presidential palace and other sensitive sites.
Why is there unrest in Niger?
Niger’s military invoked increasing armed violence to seize power in the 2023 coup. It accused the elected government of failing to quash armed rebellion.
However, three years later, armed groups remain a major threat – fighters affiliated with al-Qaeda and ISIL have continued to carry out attacks.
The military-led government boosted its ties with Russia as Niger told France and the US to withdraw their forces. Niger has also joined Burkina Faso and Mali in the AES in order to put up a united fight against armed groups.
Nevertheless, the shift has not stopped unrest. The repeated attacks and heavy military casualties have fuelled frustration among frontline troops.
ACLED’s Nsaibia described the mutiny as a sign of a wider problem.
“Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fuelling unrest within the militaries that seized power,” he said.
What has been the response of the international community?
The AES expressed support for Niger’s military leadership, saying in a statement that the mutineers had been “contained and thwarted”, calling the mutiny a “betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in a destabilisation plot”.
It was unclear whether Mali or Burkina Faso provided direct military assistance to their ally.
Algeria condemned the events and expressed its “full solidarity and firm support” for Niger.
Turkiye’s foreign ministry called for restraint and posted on X that it hoped “calm would be restored as soon as possible” while pledging to continue supporting Niger.
Why did the attack happen and what comes next?
The mutiny “speaks of deeper institutional and structural challenges within the military”, Kabir Adamu, an Abuja-based security expert, told Al Jazeera.
There is an argument that “persons who have received significant training, both within and outside [the military] are now occupying political positions and are not in the front line where they are needed to address the complex security challenges facing the country”, he said.
There are also the issues of equipment, repository, rotation of military forces.
“The grievances grew to a point where this mutiny sort of occurred,” said Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security Innovations, adding: “as part of that mutiny, based on the places they targeted, it was clearly an attempt to overthrow the government”.
“If [Tchiani] does not address the deep-rooted socioeconomic, cultural, environmental and security challenges that he promised when he took over power in July 2023, then those issues will continue to rear their head,” Adamu said.

articles.title: Iran’s Khamenei calls for Gulf unity as Hormuz tensions persist
articles.body:
Iran’s Khamenei calls for Gulf unity as Hormuz tensions persist
Khamenei urges Gulf rulers to confront their ‘real enemy’ as Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz restricted amid stalled diplomacy.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has urged Gulf leaders to identify their “real enemy” and confront it, as Tehran maintains its hard line over the Strait of Hormuz, while regional mediators push for renewed diplomacy.
“My emphatic and repeated recommendation to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia and the Gulf, is to identify your real enemy, understand his plan and confront it,” Khamenei said in a message published on Sunday to mark the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Six months into the Iran war, a new Gulf security architecture is emerging
- list 2 of 4Iran’s leaders acknowledge economic toll of war, pledge diplomacy, defence
- list 3 of 4What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
- list 4 of 4Mapping Iran war’s strikes on Gulf energy and its impact on future of oil
Khamenei has not appeared publicly since the US-Israeli attacks on February 28 that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The message comes as the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which about 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed before the war, remains unresolved.
Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that Iran had reached an understanding with Oman on a temporary maritime route, but that its implementation would depend on the United States fulfilling its commitments under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June, which has since lapsed.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed,” Gharibabadi said, adding that any vessel seeking to cross would have to coordinate with Iran.
“Implementing this understanding requires the other side, particularly the US, to fulfil its commitments. Whenever these commitments are implemented, Iran will also take its measures,” he said.
Iran and Oman have been discussing a temporary joint shipping corridor and mine clearance, while Qatar and Pakistan have intensified mediation efforts. Qatar’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani visited Tehran on Thursday, where talks included de-escalation and restoring shipping through Hormuz.
Recorded transits through the strait remain low. The Reuters news agency, citing Kpler data, said seven commodity vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15.
The International Maritime Organization said on Friday that up to 400 ships carrying about 6,000 seafarers have been unable to leave the Gulf safely since the US-Israel war on Iran began.
“Renewed political will and cooperation is needed,” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said, calling for practical measures to restore freedom of navigation through the strait.
The diplomatic push is unfolding alongside mounting economic pressure on Tehran. Iran’s annual inflation reached 66 percent last month, while President Masoud Pezeshkian said imports and exports had fallen nearly 35 percent because of US sanctions and the naval blockade.
Washington has also widened its sanctions campaign, targeting Iran-linked individuals and entities and moving to restrict the branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr bank in the United Arab Emirates from dollar transactions over alleged dealings with Tehran.
Despite the pressure, Tehran has shown no sign of yielding on Hormuz. Pezeshkian has instead called for reviving the June interim agreement with Washington.
“We can solve our problems and gain our privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei urges Muslim states to unite, oppose 'real enemy'
articles.body:
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim nations, particularly neighboring Gulf Arab states, to unite against the "real enemy," six months since the start of the Middle East war.
The message, a clear swipe at the U.S. and Israel, was published on Khamenei’s official website and Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad.
It marks his latest written communication since succeeding his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the Feb. 28 U.S.-Israeli airstrikes that launched the conflict.
The younger Khamenei, who was injured in the same attack, has not been seen in public and Iranian authorities have released no video or audio footage of him since his appointment.
Urging regional leaders to put aside political divisions, Khamenei framed internal discord as beneficial solely to foreign adversaries, asking whether the Palestinians would have been left "so helpless" had the Muslim world stood united.
"The solution to the problems of the Islamic nations is unity of words, friendship, and cooperation on the path of goodness," Khamenei wrote.
"Anyone, in any position, who does anything that leads to division among Muslims and creates conflict in the Muslim community, knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, has served the purpose of the enemies of Islam," he said.
Khamenei specifically urged the monarchies in the Persian Gulf, where relations with Tehran have frayed further following Iranian strikes on U.S. military facilities in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain during the ongoing war.
"My emphatic and repeated recommendation to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia and the Gulf, is to identify your real enemy, understand his plan and confront it," Khamenei said.
He also asked Gulf leaders whether "rogues without identity" would dare covet their lands if regional governments were "united under the flag of Islam."
Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Gulf Arab monarchies have viewed Iran's revolutionary ideology, including its anti-monarchic rhetoric and regional influence, as a threat to their political systems.
The Sunday address echoed an earlier statement Khamenei issued Friday calling for domestic solidarity and economic resilience, including a gradual de-dollarization of the Iranian economy to counter an ongoing U.S. naval blockade and long-standing economic sanctions.
"Again, this servant's advice to the Iranian people is to not allow any differences to arise among themselves in any way," Khamenei said, reiterating his warning from Friday that "doing anything detrimental to social cohesion is prohibited."

articles.title: IDF: Israel’s Apache deal not off, but at risk as NIS 15 billion delay drags on
articles.body:
With questions raised by various leaks on Sunday about whether the Finance Ministry’s delay in a NIS 15 billion payment has already broken a contract signed between Israel and the US for Apache helicopters, The Jerusalem Post was told by an IDF spokesperson that the deal is not yet off, though it may be delayed.
In January, the US State Department approved a possible $3.8b. foreign military sale to Israel of AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and related equipment. This was expected to lead to the purchase of 30 helicopters, with an initial order of 12.
Israeli defense officials had been pushing for this as a critical step toward modernizing the air force’s combat helicopter fleet, including being better prepared to use a larger fleet to prevent future potential ground invasions, such as occurred with Hamas on October 7, 2023.
Generally speaking, the air force was viewed as ineffective that day, but the helicopter fleet was one of the few bright spots in at least contributing some firepower to reducing the number of Hamas invaders in the early hours of that day.
Despite the positive move in January, delays from the ministry have already led to missed deadlines for the helicopters, notably in July.
Apache deals expected to continue, with delays
Yet another deadline was missed last Thursday.
Nevertheless, some leaks in the Hebrew media appear to exaggerate the consequences of the missed deadlines.
An IDF spokesperson said that all expectations were that the deals were still on, but simply delayed.
Delays are not free.
Often, after a delay, Israel and other countries have to pay higher fees because any deal not locked in is subject to inflation, which invariably increases the purchase price over time.
In addition, Israel's delays in purchasing additional F-15s and F-35s earlier this decade have forced Jerusalem to fall in line behind other countries that placed purchase orders. Ultimately, the delays were a much larger issue than simply the time it took Israel to make its decision.
If the first round of 12 helicopters was originally expected to begin arriving in 2030, the new arrival date could be pushed back even further than Israel's already eight-month delay.
Highly unpredictable variables, offensive weapons sales at risk
There are also highly unpredictable variables, such as whether, beyond the presidency of US President Donald Trump, which runs until January 2029, Washington will continue to sell Israel any offensive weapons it wishes to purchase.
On Thursday, Zamir blasted the ministry for what he said were politicized and unnecessary fights over budget and side financial issues.
An IDF spokesperson said there were three debates between the IDF and the ministry.
The first is that the IDF said that the ministry was due to have transferred NIS 15b. weeks ago as part of a prior deal and that the funding had been delayed.
Second, another NIS 25b. is due to be transferred imminently, but now the IDF is worried that this funding will be delayed like the earlier NIS 15b.
Third, the sides are stuck not only on the funding that was nominally already agreed to but also on future multi-year funding negotiations.
Currently, estimates have the IDF defense budget up to NIS 160b. per year, around double what it was pre-October 7.
An IDF spokesperson clarified that the NIS 40b. under debate is part of the already-agreed NIS 160b., and not related to new funding requests.
The ministry responded that the IDF should be more judicious in spending its ballooning budget.
In the past, the ministry has also accused the IDF of a mix of waste, carelessness in certain areas of spending, and, in some cases, unpoliced fraud.
The IDF has acknowledged some errors in these areas in the past, but noted that three nearly constant years of war mean its expanded budget cannot be viewed against past budgets, only against the number of fronts Israel has consistently had to fight, or be ready to fight, on.

articles.title: Ankara summons Ukraine envoy after Black Sea attacks
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone strikes a Turkish-owned roll-on/roll-off (ro-ro) cargo ship near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk earlier this month.
Türkiye summoned Ukraine’s ambassador on Aug. 29 after two Turkish-operated commercial vessels were damaged in separate drone attacks in the Black Sea near the Russian port of Tuapse, according to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources.
Ukrainian Ambassador Naryman Dzhelialov was called to the Foreign Ministry in Ankara after the attacks on the Lider Bordo Mavi and Lider Kocatepe vessels, the sources said.
The Lider Bordo Mavi was struck Aug. 26 while sailing near Tuapse, according to Turkish shipping and regional sources. The vessel, which was carrying fresh produce, caught fire after being hit by three drones, injuring five crew members.
The ship flies the Cameroon flag and is operated by a Turkish company. It had departed from the Turkish Black Sea port of Samsun around Aug. 25 and was headed for Tuapse after reportedly being unable to call at the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
The Lider Kocatepe was sent to the area the following day to assist the damaged vessel but was itself targeted by a drone while en route, according to media reports. It sustained material damage and returned to Samsun.
Ukraine did not immediately publicly claim responsibility for either attack. Russia has attributed similar recent strikes on commercial shipping to Ukrainian forces.
The incidents have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea, where civilian shipping has increasingly been exposed to the effects of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
During the meeting, Turkish officials conveyed Ankara’s concerns over the attacks and stressed the need to protect lives, property, navigation and the marine environment, the ministry sources said.
Türkiye has repeatedly warned that the war should not further threaten civilian maritime traffic or disrupt commercial navigation in the Black Sea. Türkiye has sought to maintain relations with both Russia and Ukraine while positioning itself as a mediator in efforts to limit the war’s impact on civilian and commercial activity.
The full extent of the damage to both vessels was still being assessed on Aug. 31.

articles.title: Israeli teens charged with spying for Iran for money
articles.body:
JERUSALEM, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Two Israeli teenagers, aged 14 and 16, were charged with spying and carrying out other paid assignments for an Iranian intelligence agent, Israel's police said Sunday.
The two, from the Haifa area in northern Israel, contacted the Iranian agent after one of them responded to a job offer on Telegram.
Police said the teenager later recruited his friend and the pair carried out tasks, including photographing sites in central Israel, gathering information on security arrangements, spraying anti-government graffiti, and trying to recruit other minors.
They were paid several thousand shekels in cryptocurrency, according to police.
Israel's state-owned Kan TV news reported that they also sent information on entrances and exits, as well as the number of security guards, at shopping malls in Tel Aviv and Herzliya, a city north of Tel Aviv.
The case follows a series of arrests over alleged Iranian efforts to recruit Israelis online. Israeli authorities have previously warned that Iranian operatives were approaching minors through social media with offers of payment for spying tasks.
In 2025, 25 Israelis and foreign residents were indicted for spying for Iran in 2025, and 120 Iranian espionage attempts were thwarted, according to the Shin Bet domestic security agency. ■

articles.body:
JERUSALEM/GAZA, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- An Israeli airstrike killed at least two Palestinians, including a child, in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza on Sunday, Palestinian media reported, while Israel's military said the attack targeted a Hamas militant.
In a statement, the military identified the man as Hassam Osama Hussein Nasir, whom it said belonged to Hamas' armed wing and had been planning attacks against Israeli troops. It did not comment on the reported death of the child.
Meanwhile, a senior official of the Palestinian National Liberation Movement (Fatah) urged the international community to take practical steps to halt Israeli violations in the Gaza Strip.
Munzer al-Hayek, Fatah spokesman in Gaza, told Voice of Palestine radio that the spread of diseases, coupled with shortages of medicines and medical treatment, has turned daily life into a continuous struggle for residents in the strip.
He also urged the international community to take Israel to international courts and support accountability efforts for alleged violations and crimes against the Palestinian people.
According to Gaza's health authorities, 1,318 Palestinians have been killed and 4,375 others injured in the Gaza Strip since the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in October 2025.
The overall death toll in the Gaza Strip since Oct. 7, 2023, has risen to 73,454, with 174,486 others injured, according to the authorities. ■

articles.title: IRCS, ICRC hold TOT workshop on psychological support for specialist teams
articles.body:
IRCS, ICRC hold TOT workshop on psychological support for specialist teams
TEHRAN – The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have organized a Training of Trainers (TOT) workshop on ‘Delivering Psychosocial Support for the Specialist Teams of the Iranian Red Crescent Society.’
The three-day workshop, held from August 24 to 26 in Tehran, aimed at strengthening mental health and psychosocial support for IRCS emergency responders.
It responded to the psychological pressures faced by Relief and Rescue personnel working in conflict, crisis and other high-pressure environments, the ICRC website announced in a press release on August 26.
Approximately 20 IRCS psychologists from across the country participated in the training. The workshop combined theoretical learning, practical exercises and facilitated discussions, covering responder wellbeing and resilience, peer support, identification of psychological distress, referral pathways, supportive interventions and self-care.
“The initiative follows four earlier workshops conducted last year, which trained approximately 160 IRCS first responder personnel”, Roman Paramanov, the deputy head of the ICRC delegation in Iran, said in the opening ceremony of the workshop.
The workshop used a two-phase cascade training model to extend psychosocial support across the IRCS Relief and Rescue Organization. In the first phase, participants from provinces received this three-day Training of Trainers (ToT), strengthening their skills in responder wellbeing, self-care, peer support, psychological distress identification and referral.
In the second phase, the trained psychologists work in 10 co-facilitation pairs, delivering mental self-care and psychosocial support workshops to Heads of Relief and Rescue Bases and operational personnel.
Through this cascade approach, the programme aims to reach approximately 600 IRCS staff, while ongoing supervision, online follow-up and technical support help ensure consistent application and sustainability.
Need for strategic partnership roadmap
On August 5, the IRCS deputy director for international and humanitarian law affairs, Razieh Alishvandi, in a meeting with the new president of the ICRC, Stephan Bonamy, highlighted the need to enhance cooperation to a long-term strategic partnership, proposing the development of a roadmap for collaboration.
The official also called for increasing support for relief workers, expanding technological cooperation, and utilizing extensive capabilities of the IRCS in responding to regional and international crises.
Highlighting the capabilities of the IRCS, including its vast search-and-rescue network, land and air fleets, medical and rehabilitation centers, helal (crescent) houses, massive volunteer network, training and production capacities, she stated that the IRCS is one of the most capable national societies in the region and is prepared to share its experiences and resources with other national societies.
Referring to over 200 rehabilitation centers, pharmaceutical, and medical facilities affiliated with the IRCS operating in the country, and the IRCS capabilities in manufacturing medicines, medical equipment, and relief supplies, Alishvandi proposed expanding collaborations in technology transfer, product standardization, and the utilization of the IRCS production capacity within supply chains and international humanitarian operations.
She also voiced the IRCS readiness to serve as a regional hub in fields such as rehabilitation, International Humanitarian Law training, Chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) training, crisis management, Restoring Family Links (RFL), and mass gathering management.
The official stressed the need to benefit from modern technologies, noting that the use of artificial intelligence in crisis management, hazard analysis, satellite image analysis, humanitarian data management, operational information systems, and digital crisis management can bring about a significant transformation in the quality and speed of incident response.
Moreover, Alishvandi called for the implementation of joint projects in mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), the training of specialized personnel, the development of post-crisis intervention protocols, and cooperation during regional crises.
Highlighting the development of regional cooperation regarding crisis preparedness and response, Alishvandi said developing joint emergency response scenarios, conducting collaborative exercises, pre-positioning relief supplies, and strengthening regional coordination can enhance the international movement’s preparedness for future crises.
The official also urged the ICRS to play a more constructive role in safeguarding civilians and rescuers during the conflicts.
“Support for aid workers must become a key pillar of joint efforts. Joint protection programs, specialized training on mission security, the documentation of attacks against relief personnel, and the exchange of international experiences should be put on the agenda,” she noted.
For his part, Bonamy underlined sustaining and developing the ongoing collaboration between the two organizations, lauding the ICRC the IRCS capabilities and valuable experience in relief operations, pre-hospital care, rehabilitation, international humanitarian law, and humanitarian crisis response. The official announced the ICRC willingness to expand technical and specialized cooperation between the two parties.
Expressing sympathy with the Iranians, he noted that: “We are aware of the difficult conditions people have faced in the aftermath of the war.” The ICRC will strive, within the framework of its humanitarian mandate, to effectively cooperate with the IRCS to alleviate human suffering.
Offering condolences on the martyrdom of the relief workers, he expressed sympathy with their families and the Iranian nation, highlighting that: “The loss of relief workers while carrying out humanitarian missions is a matter of deep concern to us. Red Cross and Red Crescent societies are members of a family. In such circumstances, they must stand together and support one another.”
Referring to the future plans of the ICRC, Bonamy said that cooperation with the IRCS is a cornerstone of the committee’s activities in the country, adding that enhancing preparedness to face potential crises requires close cooperation, ongoing coordination, and joint programming.
The ICRC is prepared to expand its cooperation with the IRCS in areas like search and rescue, pre-hospital services, psychosocial support, rehabilitation, the promotion of mental health for relief workers and disaster victims, and specialized training.
Referring to the economic and livelihood impacts of the US attacks on residents in southern parts of the country, particularly fishers, the official voiced the ICRC readiness to support assistance programs aimed at restoring the livelihoods of those affected.

articles.title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live on | Ed Vulliamy
articles.body:
Men age and die, but in the Balkans, time stands still and is stuck. General RatkoMladić, who died in prison in The Hague on Thursday aged 84, remains a hero in the Republika Srpska statelet – the Serbian half of dismembered Bosnia that he carved out with a hurricane of violence between 1992 and 1995 – and in Serbia itself.
Too many Serbs in whose name Mladić carried out his mass murder of other ethnicities – mainly Muslim Bošniak and Roman Catholic Croats – adore him and mourn his passing.
Since Bosnia’s war ended, Mladić’s portrait has adorned posters, gable ends, mantelpieces and football fans’ flags. Supporters of Red Star Belgrade marked his death at a match against Viktoria Plzeň on Thursday night with banners reading: “General: Eternal glory. Thank you.”
Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik extended his condolences to the Mladić family and paid tribute: “Republika Srpska will not forget his role, just as it has not forgotten it to this day. A man has died who was the commander in the struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people here, a commander who led the honourable army of Republika Srpska from the first day of its establishment. A man who demonstrated his human and military character.”
Conversely, in the 30 years since the war ended, there has been scant apology from Serbian quarters to those people, most of them Muslims, who survived Mladić’s massacres, and no reckoning. Au contraire: across Republika Srpska, hatred of what remains of “the other” and for federal authority in the capital of Sarajevo is palpable and quotidian. A friend writes to me from Bosnia: “We’re still living with the legacy every day. Listening to Republika Srpska, to Dodik, to [Serbia’s president] Vučić, the same old lies, the same old denial.” There is mass collective amnesia, denial of or – nonsensically – justification for what was done.
Mourners who gather annually at the mass cemetery of victims of the Srebrenica massacre of some 8,000 men and boys in July 1995, and for commemorations at concentration camps, are routinely harassed by police and onlookers. It is made clear to Muslims and Croats who have dared to return to Republika Srpska in the north-west and east of the bitterly divided country that, if they could, the Serbs would do it all again.
Mladić had a singular, and singularly nasty, squint. You can see it in the footage of him as he prepared the Srebrenica massacre, and in photo portraits that abound this weekend. For very many, it was a death sentence; for me, it was a stab across a courtroom at the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague as I took the witness stand in 2012 to testify against him. Having delivered that terrifying gaze, Mladić never met my eyes again during a half day of evidence from the ground of atrocities committed by those under his command. He sent a shiver of fear down the spine of anyone near him, and he knew it.
Mladić was the military wing of an unholy trinity: at its apex, Serbia’s then president, Slobodan Milošević, resurrected the insane idea of a “Greater Serbia”, a form of nationalist fascism whereby wherever the Serbs lived, only Serbs would live – everyone else would leave or die, and every vestige of their culture and religion (Muslim or Catholic) would be erased. His political co-commander in Bosnia was Radovan Karadžić, president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic. Milošević died while on trial at The Hague; like Mladić, Karadžić was convicted of genocide and other war crimes and remains jailed – surreally, on the Isle of Wight.
If Milošević and Karadžić were dangerously deranged, Mladič was bloodthirstily effective. He was the killer, the “Butcher of Bosnia”. To invoke and invert Hannah Arendt, if the others were the evil of banality, Mladić was the real thing: the banality of evil.
Mladić was a military more than an ideological man, a career officer in the Yugoslav army. He knew what he was doing. Transcripts of the Bosnian Serb assembly submitted to The Hague by an historian at the University of Michigan, Robert Donia, show Mladić expressing concern in 1992 that the political leadership was setting goals that would be hard to achieve. “We cannot cleanse, or sift with a sieve, so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how … Mr Karadžić would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide.” And so it was – at Srebrenica at least, according to The Hague tribunal – and as a good military commander, Mladić obeyed his political masters and enforced his own orders.
Mladić was convicted at The Hague in 2017. The media talked about “closure” for his victims. Wishful nonsense: there is no “closure”, nor can there be as long as the Serbs celebrate this creature.
Most discussion of Mladić since his passing has inevitably invoked Srebrenica, the infamous massacre. There is the TV footage of him smirking, knowing what was to come. But it was not only Srebrenica. Srebrenica was the most egregious war crime, but it was a denouement: more than 55,000 Muslims and 7,000 Croats had already been killed in other places over those three years, and two million had fled their homes. Foca and Višegrad (sites of rape camps for the indulgence of Mladić’s soldiers); Rogatica, Vlasenica and Sokolac; Bjeljina and Brcko, Kozarac, Sanski Most, Ključ … the list goes on. The siege of Sarajevo counted 11,541 deaths, including 1,600 children.
Mladić achieved most of what he set out to do. The “international community” granted the Bosnian Serbs a large part of what they killed, raped, tortured and burned for with the Dayton peace agreement, signed in 1995. There was baffling agreement from the Muslim-led government, apparently more anxious to establish its own sectarian fiefdom than unite the republic in a war that the Bosnian army was – actually, finally – winning by that summer (in a counteroffensive that set Mladiċ’s soldiers to flight, liberating territory then returned at Dayton to Republika Srpska).
Mladić succeeded in persecuting a very Bosnian, casually convivial interpretation of Islam into something more identitarian and polemical. In the absurd waltz of aspirant accession to the EU, Serbia leads the Balkan queue, ahead of truncated Bosnia, despite Belgrade’s open allegiance and subservience to Russia.
Above all, Mladić has succeeded in death, as he did in life, because of the adoration he still commands. His mission to establish an ethnically “pure”, fascistic Greater Serbia remains a dream, and a plan. Through public celebrations, he continues to terrorise the lives of those mostly Muslims and a few Croats brave enough to return to live under the insignia of those who mass murdered their families.
Mladić’s funeral will probably tell us more than his death. Several Serbian government officials and ministers urge a “state and military funeral, and day of mourning”. The prresident, Aleksandar Vučić, says he will leave arrangements to the general’s son, Darko, who is of the faith. If Darko decides on full national honours, that is what will happen. Mladić is dead, but lives on.
- 
  Ed Vulliamy is an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian and Observer

articles.title: Trump the renamer-in-chief keen to leave his mark – or his stain – on world
articles.body:
Is it a key policy move which will “recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people”? Or “real foolishness”?
Whatever the impact of Donald Trump unusual decision to retitle Lake Ontario as Lake America, days after Canada’s prime minister refused to be cowed by Trump’s punitive tariffs, it has certainly divided opinion – but perhaps it shouldn’t have come as a surprise.
Trump, after all, is a president who in his second term has proved himself to be the renamer-in-chief, with arguably his biggest successes coming in the area of rebranding buildings and entities, frequently after himself.
There was the United States Institute of Peace being renamed the Donald J Trump United States Institute of Peace last December. The introduction of so-called “Trump accounts” to encourage people to save money. The establishment of “TrumpRx” pharmaceutical sales. And, perhaps most hubristically, the plan to introduce “Trump-class” battleships – the largest battleships the US has created since the second world war.
Given the naming pattern, perhaps Americans can be thankful that Lake Ontario wasn’t renamed Lake Trump. The title Lake America, announced in an executive order on Thursday, strikes as a little unimaginative, a little on the nose.
That’s because the president has already done this: unilaterally and, some might say, unsuccessfully, renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America on the first day of his second term. (Eighteen months on, few serious media outlets use the term “Gulf of America”, with Trump’s order effectively only applying to the federal government, although that didn’t stop the White House from banning the Associated Press from the Oval Office in February 2025 when the news agency declined to use the term.)
In his Lake America order, Trump didn’t mention the trade spat with Canada that prompted the renaming. Instead, the president claimed: “It is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements.”
Trump went on to claim that the US “claims most of the Lake’s volume”, because the deepest part of the lake lies within US territory. “This is official, effective immediately,” he said after signing the order, although, as the Associated Press noted, the order actually says the changes must be made within 30 days.
Whether that will convince people to use the new term remains to be seen, because Trump certainly can’t force other countries to use it, and even his order is limited in scope. It directs Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, to “update the Geographic Names Information System” – basically a sort of grand online map – to “remove all references to Lake Ontario” from government materials, but it’s unclear how the government will force businesses – and states – to follow up.
While we wait to see who adopts Lake America, Trump is embroiled in an ongoing battle in his attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, in Washington. Trump fired the center’s existing board last year and appointed a group of lackeys that voted to add his name to the center.
The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts thus became the Donald J Trump and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, but, after a judge ruled Trump’s name was added illegally, went back to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in May. (Trump’s board is now attempting to rename the center the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump. Members also want to rename a plaza in front of the building after Trump.)
There are also rumblings that the Trump administration wants to rename New York City’s Penn Station after the president – a move unlikely to go down well in a city where Trump is deeply unpopular.
In the meantime, the response to the newly rebranded Lake America has been tepid.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” Kathy Hochul, the state’s governor, responded to a White House social media post announcing the change. Given Lake Ontario’s only US border is the state of New York, Hochul’s opposition could cause a problem, although it will surely be welcomed by New York-based cruise companies whose marketing materials use the term Lake Ontario.
Canadians are also unimpressed.
Asked about Trump’s move during a press conference on Thursday, Wab Kinew, the premier of Manitoba, was withering in his assessment.
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago? I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said.
“He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”

articles.title: Regulating weapons 'purely Iraqi decision,' says Badr Organization chief
articles.body:
Emre Demiral and Serdar Dincel
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
The leader of Iraq’s Badr Organization, Hadi al-Amiri, said Sunday that regulating weapons in the country is a “purely Iraqi decision,” ruling out any possible confrontation between the state and the “resistance.”
“I guarantee everyone that there will be absolutely no clash between the state and the resistance," Amiri said in a speech carried by the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
“Regulating weapons is a legitimate national and constitutional goal and a foundation for building a strong state capable of protecting Iraq and preserving its sovereignty," he added.
Amiri said fighting corruption was a decision agreed upon by the Coordination Framework, a coalition of Shiite parties, reiterating support for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s anti-corruption campaign.
The issue of weapons outside state control is among Iraq’s most prominent security and political challenges, amid the presence of armed factions, some of which are affiliated with the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), while others operate independently.
The PMF is an official Iraqi security umbrella established in 2014 following a religious edict by top cleric Ali al-Sistani to confront ISIS (Daesh) terrorists, and was later integrated into the armed forces by a government decision in 2016.
In June, Iraqi military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced the establishment of a committee tasked with overseeing efforts to bring unregulated weapons under state control.

articles.title: Turkish, Somali forces free hijacked vessel from pirates
articles.body:
A soldier from the Turkiye Somali Naval Task Group stands guard.
Türkiye’s navy, along with Somali armed forces, have freed a hijacked vessel held in Somali waters and killed 14 pirates after a battle lasting several days, Mogadishu’s government said on Aug. 29.
The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year, the highest since 2013.
“During the ten-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed,” said a Somali Defense Ministry statement.
“The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship,” it added.
“The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey.”
According to sources in Puntland, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turk.
The Marine Traffic website shows that the vessel, which operates under a Cameroonian flag, left Türkiye in late July bound for the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam.
The joint Türkiye-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.
Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somalia in the 2000s, peaking in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.
But attacks have surged since April, with at least five cargo ships held hostage, the last of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

articles.title: Incidents of AI going rogue double – Guardian
articles.body:
Incidents of AI going rogue double – Guardian
A record number of instances of artificial intelligence (AI) lying, ignoring users’ commands or acting in harmful ways to achieve its goals were registered last month, The Guardian has reported, citing a monitoring group.
Concerns about the safety of AI are on the rise after advanced models by OpenAI and Anthropic exhibited rogue behavior during testing this summer, with calls made to halt their development and introduce stricter government oversight of the process.
There were more than 300 incidents of real-world loss of control involving AI models employed by actual businesses and private individuals in July, which is almost double the number in June, an article in the paper said on Saturday.
The data came from the Loss of Control Observatory, which was set up by the UK government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) last November to track complaints about issues with AI made by users on X, it said.
As the monitor only gathers reports from a single social media platform, the true number of incidents must be higher, The Guardian noted.
A majority out of the 1,600 complaints on X in 2026 were made by software developers using AI bots in their work, according to AISI.
The monitor said that despite the fact that most real-world loss of control incidents did not cause significant harm, it has registered an increase in severity of AI’s deceptiveness and neglect of human commands.
Reports by users “evidence AI systems’ willingness to disregard direct instructions, circumvent safeguards, lie to users and single-mindedly pursue a goal in harmful ways,” AISI warned.
Tommy Shaffer-Shane, the senior policy manager at the Centre for Long Term Resilience, which operates the observatory, told The Guardian that it is wrong to suggest that AI only misbehaves during testing.
“We need to not be complacent that these things won’t happen in the real world and there is evidence that they already are,” he said.
The monitor has called on the British government to oblige AI companies to report loss of control incidents and to introduce emergency powers, including temporary restrictions on artificial intelligence, in order to deal with the more severe cases.

articles.title: Why is 'vegan' suddenly being used as a slur? | Emma Beddington
articles.body:
Cool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble, tofu-eating wokerati to dangerous radicals unfit for public office. Politico reports that US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,” Trump warned of Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is “neither man nor woman”.)
Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretary described him on X as “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowa drew heat for merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”.
It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does America actually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official response to “vegan accusations” (“accusations” – the word you’d use for say, corruption or sexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’s first indictment” (despite many years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime).
Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”.
Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office.
Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle.
And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome.
Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s 2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of the landmark 2018 study on the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes, concluded that excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”.
Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist
