articles.title: Istanbul to host 1st Mecca Pact meeting
articles.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan speaks with his Saudi Arabian counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, ahead of a meeting.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will hold the first meeting of a committee established under a joint defense pact in Istanbul on Aug. 31, as the three countries seek to deepen military cooperation and coordinate on regional security.
The Strategic Political and Defense Committee’s inaugural meeting is expected to bring together the foreign and defense ministers and military chiefs of the three countries, according to Turkish diplomatic sources.
Türkiye is expected to be represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu.
Pakistan’s delegation is expected to include Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Federal Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and Army Chief Asim Munir. Saudi Arabia is expected to send Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili.
The committee was established to provide strategic direction for activities under the Mecca Joint Defense Pact, signed by the leaders of the three countries earlier this month.
The meeting is expected to address international security issues and efforts to strengthen the defense capabilities of the three countries and improve interoperability among their armed forces, the sources said.
Participants are also expected to discuss deeper cooperation in the defense industry, including joint production and research and development, as well as stronger joint counterterrorism efforts.
The committee is expected to establish a framework for a secretariat and other mechanisms to coordinate work in areas of joint activity. It will also seek to draw up a roadmap for implementing the pact in the coming period, according to the sources.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif signed the pact in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The agreement was signed amid what officials described as growing instability in the countries’ regions and internationally. It seeks to promote security, peace, stability and prosperity while strengthening the three countries’ joint deterrence capabilities.
The pact stipulates that “an attack against any one of the parties will be considered an attack against all parties.”
The three countries have sought to expand defense ties in recent years, including through military exercises, defense industry cooperation and diplomatic coordination.
Ankara slams Israeli statement
Meanwhile, Türkiye on Aug. 29 rejected an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement targeting Erdoğan, saying the “lies and slanders” in it reflected the mentality of officials serving in the Israeli government.
“The statement issued by the Israeli Foreign Ministry reflects the cowardly and rotten mentality of the criminals serving in the Israeli government, particularly [Benjamin] Netanyahu,” Ankara said.
The statement accused Erdoğan of being antisemitic and of inciting hostility toward Israel.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said Netanyahu and his “criminal network” had brought “historic shame” on the Israeli people through what it described as genocide in Gaza.
“The immunities enjoyed by Netanyahu and his criminal network are disappearing both legally and politically,” it added.

articles.title: Why some young people stick with social causes while others fade away
articles.body:
Young adults in the United States who support social causes due to internal moral convictions are more likely to anticipate staying engaged over time than those driven by a desire for social approval. Research published in Social Psychology Quarterly indicates that political ideology shapes these motivations, with liberals often acting from empathy and conservatives frequently relying on community approval. The researchers found that external motivations can still foster lasting commitment when tied to enduring social networks like religious groups.
When people participate in social, political, or religious causes, their reasons for getting involved typically fall into two categories. Internal motivation involves a deep personal commitment or moral dedication to an issue. External motivation involves acting to gain social approval or avoid punishment.
External motivation is often debated under the term performative activism on social media. Observers often view performative activism as actions that have minimal actual impact while maximizing public visibility for the person performing them.
Psychologists classify these motivational differences using self-determination theory. This framework suggests that while both internal and external motivations can prompt short-term action, internally motivated behaviors are generally more persistent.
Researchers E. Ashby Plant and Kyle Rose of Florida State University led a team to explore how these motivational sources affect participation among young adults. The researchers wanted to understand whether specific emotional responses to social causes encourage people to act for internal or external reasons. They also sought to determine how a person’s political ideology might influence their emotional and motivational approaches to social engagement.
The research team began by conducting a survey of 934 young adults between the ages of 18 and 29. The participants answered questions about their online and offline involvement in political, religious, and civic activities over the past year. They also rated their intended engagement in these areas over the next twelve months.
Each person identified a primary cause that mattered most to them. They then rated statements assessing their internal and external motivations to act. For example, they indicated whether they promoted the cause because it was personally important or because they wanted to gain approval from others.
The participants also provided their political orientation and rated how strongly they felt certain emotions when thinking about their primary cause. The researchers categorized these emotions as either self-focused, such as pride and guilt, or other-focused, such as empathy and anger directed at wrongdoers.
The survey results showed that both internal and external motivations were associated with participants taking action in the past. When predicting future behavior, however, only internal motivation was linked to intended ongoing engagement.
Emotions played a distinct role in these motivational pathways. Participants with high internal motivation tended to experience other-focused emotions, alongside feeling positive about themselves and reporting lower levels of guilt. Those with high external motivation were more likely to report self-focused emotions, including both pride and guilt.
Political ideology strongly influenced these patterns. Liberal participants reported higher levels of empathy, negative emotions directed at others, and internal motivation. The data indicated that their tendency to experience empathy and anger statistically accounted for their higher internal motivation.
Conservative participants reported higher levels of pride and external motivation. The researchers found that feelings of pride statistically explained their tendency to rely on external motivation for their activism.
To gain deeper insight into these survey patterns, the researchers conducted follow-up interviews with 30 of the participants. They selected ten liberals, ten moderates, and ten conservatives to answer open-ended questions about their motivations and feelings regarding social engagement. Two independent researchers coded the interview transcripts to identify expressions of motivation and emotion.
During the interviews, liberal participants frequently emphasized their internal motivations and explicitly rejected the idea of acting for social reputation. They framed their participation as a moral responsibility and expressed anger about injustice, along with frustration toward people who remained apathetic.
Liberal interviewees also highlighted the emotional toll of their activism. As one liberal participant explained about managing anger, “There’s two types of anger. There’s anger that fuels you, and there’s anger that burns you.”
Conservative participants often described their engagement in terms of social interaction and community building. Many of these respondents tied their activism to their religious faith, which provided a supportive network that encouraged their involvement.
These individuals often expressed pride and satisfaction in seeing the tangible results of their group’s efforts, such as distributing donations to people in need. Another participant described the tangible satisfaction of directly helping people, such as bringing coats to those in need, saying, “It feels like, okay, this is actually making a difference.”
The interview responses suggested that the traditional divide between internal and external motivation might be less rigid for individuals motivated by faith. For many conservative participants, a desire for approval from their religious community or God functioned as a highly stable form of external motivation.
The study relied on survey data collected at a single point in time, which restricts the researchers from establishing a cause-and-effect relationship between emotion, motivation, and engagement. People’s feelings and motivations might evolve as they spend more time participating in a cause.
Participants reported their own past and future behaviors, which can sometimes differ from objective reality. Tracking actual activities, such as measuring the time spent on specific digital platforms or logging attendance at community events, could provide a more accurate picture of engagement.
Finally, the external motivation driven by a religious community might operate differently than external motivation aimed at impressing peers or the general public. A religious community or a belief in an ever-present deity might offer a permanent audience, making that specific type of external motivation unusually stable over time.
The study, “Social Engagement for Oneself and Others: The Roles of Motivation, Emotion, and Political Ideology,” was authored by E. Ashby Plant, Kyle Rose, Yuki Maynor, Levi Mitzen, Bayla K. Thompson, Deana A. Rohlinger, and Grant W. Bailey.

articles.title: South Africa urges ICJ to act on Israel's ongoing Gaza violence
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
South Africa urges ICJ action over Israel's non-compliance with Gaza orders
South Africa has submitted a dossier to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing Israel of continuing to disregard court orders intended to protect Palestinians amid the Gaza conflict, which is set to enter its third year.
The South African Foreign Ministry said on Friday that the dossier was submitted on 25 August to assist a committee of judges responsible for monitoring the implementation of provisional measures and recommending possible action to the court.
Pretoria said it presented the evidence after concluding that Israel had failed to comply with three legally binding provisional measures issued by the ICJ to protect the rights of Palestinians under the Genocide Convention.
South Africa launched legal proceedings against Israel at the ICJ on 29 December 2023, alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court subsequently issued three separate provisional measures orders on 26 January, 28 March and 24 May 2024, after South Africa requested urgent intervention over the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
The rulings required Israel to take all necessary measures to prevent acts prohibited under the convention.
The court also ordered Israel to implement safeguards against potential genocidal acts, halt military operations in the southern Gaza city of Rafah where such operations could cause physical destruction to the Palestinian population, and provide regular reports on its compliance with the measures.
In its latest statement, South Africa said it would continue pursuing “all avenues available” to seek Israel’s full and immediate compliance with the court’s orders.
“Regrettably, Israel has not complied with the Orders,” Pretoria stated in the filing.
South Africa warned that the rights of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip could be “destroyed before [the ICJ] renders its final decision”, a situation it said threatened the "legitimacy of the ICJ itself".
The dossier stated that, as of August, at least 73,407 Palestinians had been killed and 174,335 injured, together representing "over 10% of the Palestinian population" of the Gaza Strip.
It also said that, since the announcement of a "so-called ‘ceasefire" in October 2025 the Israeli military had killed an average of one Palestinian child per day.
The submission further stated that miscarriage rates among Palestinian women had "increased more than three-fold" in 2026.
South Africa also said that Israel had “arbitrarily detained and deported Palestinians” who were subsequently “tortured, subjected to sexual and gender-based violence, and to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment”.
The department additionally accused Israel of killing local journalists and preventing foreign journalists and UN-mandated investigative bodies from entering Gaza.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, despite rights groups warning that the scale and nature of its violence, including killings, restrictions on humanitarian aid, mass displacement and the destruction of medical services, could amount to genocidal acts.
Rights groups have also pointed to statements by Israeli officials that they say indicate genocidal intent.
Despite a ceasefire in Gaza that has been in place since October 2025, Israeli attacks have continued across the devastated Palestinian enclave. Israel's military has killed at least 1,313 Palestinians since then, according to Gaza's health ministry.

articles.title: How attention deficit hyperactivity disorder shapes sexual experiences
articles.body:
Adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder often face distinct challenges in maintaining sexual satisfaction and connection with their partners. A recent analysis of personal accounts from people with the condition revealed that characteristics such as a heightened need for novelty and difficulty regulating focus can deeply influence their intimate lives. The findings were published in the journal Archives of Sexual Behavior.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in executive functioning. This term refers to the mental skills involved in working memory, flexible thinking, and self-control. People with the condition often experience variations in how their brains produce and respond to dopamine. Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in reward processing, motivation, and physical arousal.
Because of these neurological differences, the condition frequently manifests as distractibility, impulsivity, and a heightened drive to seek out new experiences. These traits can create friction in social settings and intimate partnerships. Previous assessments have indicated that this population generally reports lower levels of sexual satisfaction compared to those without the diagnosis. Yet few investigations have explored exactly how these individuals perceive and navigate their own intimate encounters.
To understand the lived experiences behind these statistics, researchers Annelil E. Desille of the Institute for Social Neuroscience in Australia and Beatrice Alba of Deakin University gathered personal testimonies. They wanted to identify the specific ways that neurological differences shape both sexual satisfaction and the interactions that follow sexual activity. Understanding these perspectives could eventually help mental health professionals provide better guidance for patients facing relationship difficulties.
The researchers recruited 98 adults who reported having a formal diagnosis of the condition from a health practitioner. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 64, with the majority residing in Australia or the United States. To confirm the presence and severity of their symptoms, all participants completed a standard self-report screening questionnaire. The study group included 72 women, 17 men, and eight non-binary individuals.
Through an anonymous online survey, the respondents answered five open-ended questions about their consensual sexual experiences. They were prompted to describe their overall satisfaction, their motivations, and how they communicate with partners. They were also asked to identify specific factors that affect their satisfaction and detail how they act immediately after sex. The researchers chose a written format to reduce social pressure, allowing participants to answer sensitive questions honestly.
Desille and Alba analyzed the written responses by looking for recurring patterns and underlying ideas. They organized the data into three primary themes that capture the varied ways participants experience intimacy.
The first theme highlighted a tension between cooperation and disconnection within relationships. Some participants described highly satisfying experiences rooted in teamwork. In these cases, mutual effort, open communication, and a shared emotional connection fostered intimacy. Respondents noted that having a partner who accommodated their needs or shared their diagnosis helped them feel secure and sexually fulfilled.
Conversely, other respondents reported deep dissatisfaction stemming from a loss of sexual interest in their partners. Some described a habit of suppressing their own needs to please someone else out of a fear of rejection. Others expressed frustration over an inability to maintain interest in a partner after the initial excitement of a new relationship faded. These participants often felt bored or unfulfilled when their specific relational needs were not met.
A second theme centered on how individuals behave after sexual activity concludes. The responses revealed a split in how participants seek a sense of security during this vulnerable time. Many described a strong desire to connect through physical affection, cuddling, and conversation. These individuals reported that discussing what they enjoyed about the encounter helped them feel grounded and present.
On the other hand, a portion of the group detailed an urge to withdraw immediately after intimacy. Some respondents dealt with insecurity or sensory overload by independently focusing on daily tasks, showering, or looking at their phones. These opposing reactions highlight how the condition can amplify a person’s need to either intensely seek out reassurance or abruptly distance themselves to regain emotional balance.
The final theme captured the direct impact of cognitive and behavioral traits on sexual encounters. Participants frequently mentioned how a need for novelty and experimentation shaped their desires. They expressed a preference for trying new things to keep their brains engaged during intimacy.
They also described the challenge of staying present in the moment. Respondents noted that distractibility, sensory overload, and everyday stress often disrupted their focus and diminished their enjoyment. One participant expressed the need to “somehow keep my attention on the task at hand and not having it drift off into space, and being able to push through the sensory overload to climax.” Overcoming these cognitive hurdles required immense mental energy, which occasionally turned intimacy into a source of stress rather than pleasure.
The study relies on subjective, self-reported accounts, which provide insight into personal experiences but cannot establish the prevalence of these challenges across the broader population. The researchers also noted that their participant group was heavily skewed toward women. Future research would benefit from a more balanced demographic sample to see if these themes hold true across different genders.
The analysis did not account for whether participants were taking medication at the time of the survey. Pharmacological treatments are a common approach to managing the condition and could alter a person’s focus and emotional regulation during intimate encounters. Medications can also cause physical side effects that independently affect sexual functioning and satisfaction.
The researchers also did not track the presence of other mental health conditions, such as anxiety or depression. These conditions frequently co-occur with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and can influence a person’s sexual satisfaction and relationship dynamics. Documenting these concurrent conditions in future studies could help isolate which relationship challenges are specifically tied to executive functioning differences.
The study, “It’s Not You, “It’s Me”: Sexual Experiences and Sexual Satisfaction in an ADHD Sample,” was authored by Annelil E. Desille and Beatrice Alba.

articles.title: 'We never thought they were Muslims': Mohan Bhagwat recalls 1996 Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
articles.body:
'We never thought they were Muslims': Mohan Bhagwat recalls 1996 Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
Edited by: Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 30, 2026, 15:55 IST
Comments

Text Size
Small

RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat addresses at 'One World One Humanity' event, in New York on Saturday. (One World One Humanity/ ANI Video Grab)
NEW DELHI: Nearly three decades after one of the world’s deadliest aviation disasters, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat returned to the memory of the Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision in Haryana.He recalled the chaos that followed the crash. He spoke of injured passengers, bodies that had to be recovered and families arriving from far away, searching for their loved ones and trying to identify those they had lost. And he remembered the RSS volunteers who, according to him, reached the site and began helping.They treated the injured. They helped recover the dead. They assisted relatives who arrived later. They also helped arrange funeral rites.Many of the victims were Muslims. But Bhagwat said that was never a consideration for the volunteers who were serving them.Speaking at the "One World One Humanity" event in New York on Saturday, Bhagwat recalled the tragedy as an example of what he described as the RSS's philosophy of unconditional humanitarian service."Two planes collided over Haryana, which is part of Bharat, over the place named Dadri. Both were from Arab countries. Most of the passengers were Muslims. After that collision, our Swayamsevaks reached there first, and they served. Served in treating the injured... Recovering their bodies, arranging for the funeral rites when their relatives come, helping them in identifying. We never thought at that time that these were Muslims," said the RSS Chief.
The disaster took place on November 12, 1996. A Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakhstan Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 collided in the skies over Charkhi Dadri, Haryana.There were no survivors.All 349 people aboard the two aircraft were killed. The crash became the deadliest mid-air collision in aviation history.For Bhagwat, the tragedy was not only about the terrible loss of life. It was also about what happened after the aircraft came down.He recalled a moment when grief and devastation had stripped away every distinction between people. Those at the crash site needed help. Families needed answers. The dead needed dignity.Bhagwat said the volunteers did not ask who the victims were before helping them.He also said the RSS did not publicise such work because it did not expect anything in return."The prominent working organisation was RSS. We could do this because we are not in politics. And we don't go on making these things famous because we don't want anything from this. No return... In Sangha, we only give. We don't want anything. That is why in publicity matters, we are way behind."The RSS chief was speaking in New York as he began a three-nation global outreach tour covering the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. The visit has been organised as part of the organisation's centenary year celebrations, following invitations from overseas local organisations.Bhagwat also used the occasion to speak about perceptions of the RSS. He said the organisation was often viewed through narratives that, in his view, did not reflect its work on the ground."There are many perceptions created by wrong narratives. But when you come and see us from inside, all those will be disbelieved in the day."He then broadened his argument beyond the RSS and its work during disasters. He spoke about the kind of social change he believes is necessary to create greater unity.Bhagwat said political systems alone could not bring about such change. In a democracy, he argued, political leaders ultimately respond to public opinion. The first step, therefore, had to be taken within society itself."Politics today, especially in a democracy, depends on the public view. If there is public opinion, then no politician will dare to go against it. Therefore, I think after taking a common resolve today, we have to act in these societies, and we have to act first locally."He argued that social harmony could not be built simply by gaining political power. It had to grow from everyday interactions and acts of service.For Bhagwat, the idea was rooted in what he described as the traditional thought of Bharat, where the unity of humanity is placed above individual interests."This is the traditional thought of Bharat--unity of humanity. All our leaders, at any point in time, have emphasised that too. After independence, we got the constitution, which emphasises this, but that is not happening. Because these things do not happen through politics. I'm sorry to say, but the fact is, politics has now become a game of self-interest. And where there is me and I, there is no solution. We and ours are the solution. So our experience in Bharat is that we have to start with society."He called for such efforts to begin locally. Small pockets of people working together, he said, could eventually become larger networks of service and unity."Whatever we decide to do today, we should start in our own country and create pockets of such selfless service, such an atmosphere of unity, and then this dialogue should continue. Through this dialogue, we should connect them, and then we should grow."
Nearly 30 years after the Charkhi Dadri crash, the scale of the disaster remains difficult to comprehend. Hundreds of lives were lost in a matter of moments.But Bhagwat chose to remember what happened in the aftermath.Amid the wreckage, he said, volunteers came forward to help people they did not know. They treated the injured. They recovered bodies. They helped families search for answers.And, in his telling of that day, they did so without first asking whether the person in front of them was Hindu or Muslim.That memory formed the emotional centre of Bhagwat's message in New York: that in moments of profound human suffering, service can begin before identity does.

articles.title: Palestinian Christians are disappearing. Warnings are not enough.
articles.body:
I was born and raised in Jerusalem, and I still live here. Growing up, I do not remember my generation or my father’s sorting friends and neighbors by religion. I never thought of Issam, my friend, as “the Christian,” or Nizar, my next-door neighbor, as “the Muslim.”
At some point, however, a strange new phrase entered our vocabulary: “our Christian brothers, our partners in the homeland.” I never liked it. Why “partners”? They were never anything other than an indigenous part of this country — milh hadha al-ard, or “the salt of the earth,” as we say in Arabic.
I feel the same discomfort with slogans such as “we seek national unity between Palestinian Muslims and Christians.” Such slogans often end up proving the opposite of what they intend — as though we first have to establish that people who have lived together for centuries are, in fact, one people.
This matters because the decline of the Palestinian Christian presence is real, serious, and accelerating — and the response remains largely stuck at the level of warning. Every few months, church leaders, activists, and the Palestinian media return to the same message: Christians are disappearing. But there is no plan to confront that decline.
Today, roughly 47,000 to 50,000 Christians remain in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian Bureau of Statistics figures from 2017, and probably fewer today. Gaza had close to 1,500 Christians before the war; fewer than 500 are believed to remain, though no precise figure is possible amid displacement, killing, and the destruction of institutions and records.
This decline does not happen all at once. It happens quietly: a young Christian Palestinian from Jerusalem leaves to study and does not return; a couple builds a life in Chile rather than Bethlehem; a family in Ramallah moves to Houston, having concluded that building a future at home has simply become too difficult. The reasons are clear to all: occupation, the permit regime, expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, severe restrictions on movement, fragmented territory, economic pressure, and the absence of political prospects. This is the cage — the open prison — in which Palestinians live. But explaining Christian emigration only through that prism is no longer enough.
Before going further, it is important to acknowledge what has already been done. More than 15 years ago, Kairos Palestine offered a different vision, beginning with its 2009 document and developing into a theological and political movement and an international advocacy platform. Its message was clear: Palestinian Christians are not a separate minority waiting to be rescued from outside. They are an indigenous, deeply rooted part of the Palestinian people. Remaining on the land and resisting its dispossession, Kairos Palestine argued, are both political and theological responsibilities. With that voice, Kairos took Palestine into churches and Christian communities abroad, calling for advocacy, political pressure, and boycott, while insisting that emigration should not become an inevitable fate.
The problem, then, is not a lack of vision. There is a language of steadfastness and an international advocacy network. What is missing is the institutional and economic infrastructure that makes staying possible. It is easy to tell a young Palestinian: “Stay on your land.” The harder part is answering the questions that follow: Where will I work? Can I afford a home? How will I educate my children, start a business, and what happens when my home is demolished, or when I cannot reach my university or workplace?
This is where the churches have a particular responsibility. They possess resources most Palestinian civil-society organizations do not: valuable land and properties, schools, hospitals, guesthouses, financial resources, and international networks. Church property cannot be treated simply as an internal administrative matter. The battles over historic properties around Jaffa Gate in Jerusalem demonstrated the consequences of losing strategically important Palestinian Christian land. The lesson should be clear: the wider community cannot be called upon only after a property has been lost. Major sales and long-term leases of Palestinian Christian property should be subject to independent local review involving community representatives and Palestinian experts in law, finance, and real estate. Palestinian Orthodox Arabs have demanded a greater role in church affairs for generations — that the reform is difficult is not a reason to avoid it.
The same principle should apply to church-run schools, hospitals, and vocational institutions. Scholarships could prioritize fields needed by the Palestinian economy, and vocational programs could equip young people to earn a living without leaving. Churches connected to the pilgrimage and religious tourism industry could work deliberately to keep more of that revenue in the local economy — supporting Palestinian tourist guides, guesthouses, restaurants, transport providers, and small businesses.
No one should overstate what churches can accomplish. A scholarship does not create a job, and a training certificate does not remove a checkpoint. Churches cannot end the occupation or create a Palestinian state. But they can decide whether the resources they control remain disconnected services or become part of a coherent strategy for community survival.
The thirteen church denominations in Palestine do not need to merge, and that is clearly not realistic. They need to coordinate and divide responsibilities according to their strengths. The Orthodox Patriarchate, because of its property holdings, has a particular responsibility for defending church-owned land. Catholic institutions can do more in education and vocational training. Anglican and Protestant churches, with their international networks, can take a stronger role in legal advocacy, residency, family reunification, and international pressure.
The diaspora is another largely untapped resource. Palestinian Christians in the Americas, Europe, and the Arab world possess capital, expertise, and business networks. The question is where they are when it comes to providing small-business loans, housing assistance, youth projects, and investment in Palestinian Christian communities — in Bethlehem, Beit Jala, Beit Sahour, Jerusalem, Taybeh, Zababdeh, and elsewhere. Perhaps more urgently: where are they when it comes to the rapidly disappearing Palestinian Christian community in Gaza? What is required is capital, competent management, transparency, and will.
Palestinian civil society, business associations, professional bodies, political leaders, and Muslim institutions should also be part of a national effort to protect the Christian presence. The decline of Christians is part of the wider Palestinian crisis of land, movement, employment, and demographics. There should be practical Muslim-Christian mechanisms to defend families facing displacement, support local businesses, and advocate for threatened communities.
Western solidarity also needs to change. “Save the Christians of the Holy Land” is an emotionally powerful message, but it can obscure the larger reality: Palestinians — Muslim and Christian — are being pushed to leave by occupation and the conditions it creates. The better message is: help Palestinians remain on their land, and help Palestinian Christians build a future there. That means supporting housing, vocational education, small businesses, legal defense, land protection, and community institutions — not simply producing another report documenting how many Christians have left.
It is time for Palestinian churches to measure their role and impact differently: How many families did they help stay? How many homes were restored? How many young people were trained and helped to find work? How much land was protected? These are the real markers.
The demographic decline of Palestinian Christians is real and painful. Occupation is the cause, and while churches cannot end it, that does not absolve them of responsibility for what they can do. They have land, institutions, money, schools, international networks, and a diaspora. Kairos Palestine gave Palestinian Christian steadfastness a language and a political voice. What is needed now is to turn that message into an institutional and economic project that makes staying in the birthplace of Jesus a viable choice.
For years, we have asked: how many Christians are left? How many have left? The right question is different: what have we done to ensure that the Palestinian Christian family can remain rooted in its home, its land, and its homeland?

articles.title: Interview: China a major strategic partner for Kyrgyzstan, says Kyrgyz FM
articles.body:
BISHKEK, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev hailed China as one of Kyrgyzstan's major strategic partners in a recent interview with Xinhua prior to Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the country.
Under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state and through the joint efforts of the two governments, it's believed that the China-Kyrgyzstan comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era will continue to consolidate, bringing tangible benefits to the two peoples and making important contributions to peace, stability and sustainable development in the region, said Kulubaev.
Kulubaev noted that China has maintained close high-level political dialogue with Kyrgyzstan, and exchanges between the two governments and legislative bodies have continued to deepen, while interactions between local governments and business communities have expanded.
Cooperation in trade and the economy, investment, transport and logistics, energy, agriculture and other areas has also steadily advanced, Kulubaev said, adding that a number of joint projects currently under way are of long-term significance not only to the two countries, but also to the wider region.
"The construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is an important project of strategic significance. It will significantly improve regional connectivity, enhance Kyrgyzstan's transit transportation potential, and create new opportunities for trade and investment development," he said.
Looking ahead, he said the two countries have considerable potential to expand cooperation in such areas as the digital economy, high technology, green development, artificial intelligence, e-commerce and innovation.
Kulubaev spoke highly of China's development achievements over the past several decades, pointing to advances in economic and social development, improvements in people's living standards, scientific and technological progress, innovation and industrial modernization.
"China's development helps strengthen global economic and trade ties, promote international infrastructure construction, expand investment cooperation, and create new opportunities for developing countries," he stressed.
In his view, China's experience in formulating long-term strategic plans, supporting science and innovation, strengthening infrastructure construction and improving governance is of significant reference value to countries of the Global South.
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). Over the past 25 years, the SCO has developed into one of the world's largest international organizations and a key force in building a multipolar world order, providing a platform for equal dialogue, respect for each other's interests and joint efforts to seek solutions, Kulubaev noted.
As founding members of the SCO, China and Kyrgyzstan, together with other member states, have consistently supported efforts to enhance the organization's authority and practical effectiveness, making important contributions to its development and growth, Kulubaev said.
The 2026 SCO Summit will soon be held in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan. Kulubaev expressed confidence that the summit will inject new impetus into the SCO's development, and provide an opportunity for member states to enhance mutual trust, deepen practical cooperation and reaffirm their commitment to the "Shanghai Spirit." ■

articles.title: ‘A warning saved my life’: can Hongkongers trust smartwatches, or are they being misled?
articles.body:
‘A warning saved my life’: can Hongkongers trust smartwatches, or are they being misled?
Medical practitioners and fitness experts say wearable tech could support personalised, proactive healthcare as adoption hits 63 per cent among Hongkongers
Alice Wong had little idea how seriously ill she might become until unusual patterns on her smartwatch prompted her to seek medical advice.
A year ago, Wong, who was still in her twenties, had bought the device but paid little attention to it. That changed when she received an unusual notification warning her of an irregular heart rhythm.
What followed was a health scare and a visit to a local doctor, who diagnosed her with atrial fibrillation, or AF – an irregular heart rhythm in which the atria, the heart’s upper chambers, beat chaotically. The condition can reduce the heart’s efficiency and significantly increase the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart failure.
“I am a young and fit adult. I exercise regularly and have never previously had a serious medical episode. I don’t go for medical check-ups often, so I dread to think what could have happened if my device had not picked this up,” said Wong, who has since begun taking medication and expects to make a full recovery.
While medical practitioners, fitness experts and technology developers told the South China Morning Post that wearable devices had significant potential to support personalised and proactive healthcare, some also warned against misusing the technology or treating wearables as substitutes for doctors.
Commercial wearable technology differs from medical-grade wearables and diagnostic tools. It generally focuses on health and lifestyle tracking, monitoring metrics such as exercise, heart rate and sleep.

articles.title: UK asks banks for feelgood stories about keeping out dirty money
articles.body:
The government is asking bankers and lawyers to provide feelgood stories about how they blocked dirty money from entering the UK, as ministers try to prove the UK’s money-laundering controls are working.
The Treasury’s call for evidence is meant to illustrate that the UK has upped its game when it comes to preventing financial crime, particularly since its last dismal assessment by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) global crime watchdog in 2018, which fuelled allegations that London had become a hub for “dirty money”.
“To build the strongest possible picture of system-wide effectiveness,” the government call for evidence said, “we are looking for real-life examples with clear, demonstrable results that illustrate how the UK’s anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and sanctions frameworks operate effectively in practice.”
The government is rushing to collect those examples before it submits its own evidence packet to the taskforce in October. The watchdog’s assessment team will then visit the UK for an on-the-ground review next summer.
But the UK faces an uphill battle to prove the City has made substantial changes, and are staying alert to new threats including a surge in AI-fuelled investment fraud and the growing popularity of cryptocurrencies, which can help shield the source of transactions.
Last year, the National Crime Agency estimated that £100bn is being laundered through or within the UK every single year, with City firms providing legal and financial services for fraudsters, human traffickers, the illegal drug trade and other types of organised crime. The UK’s national risk assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing has also classed the UK legal sector as “high risk” for every one of its assessments since 2017.
“As the UK approaches its next FATF mutual evaluation in 2027, the pressure on its anti-money laundering (AML) regime is intensifying,” the rating agency Moody’s said in a report published earlier this year. “Billions are spent each year in the UK on supervision with hundreds of firms refused entry to the financial system following due diligence, yet an estimated £100bn is still laundered annually.”
Moody’s added: “When FATF examiners arrive in the UK, they may ask how much of that risk is really being reduced by the UK’s controls, intelligence and enforcement, and how quickly.”
The first phase of the next FATF review will allow the UK government to submit its own evidence, outlining how effectively the country handles and prevents money laundering and other financial crime.
The Treasury is asking City firms to share any cases, from 2022 onward, showing how they dumped, or refused to take on, potentially high-risk clients. That is on top of cases where a company’s intervention later led to a state investigation or prosecution.
The government has also asked companies for any examples where they discovered red flags for financial crime in customer profiles, and how this ended up changing the types of clients the firm was willing to take on.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We take firm and coordinated action across government and industry to crack down on economic crime. We have introduced new strategies, enhanced enforcement capabilities and increased funding designed to disrupt those seeking to abuse the UK economy.
“As you would expect, the government regularly engages with industry on this - and preparations for the FATF assessment in 2027 are no different.”

articles.title: Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?
articles.body:

Opinion
Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?
China’s measured stance since the Xi-Trump summit in May is reaching a tipping point as US pressure mounts
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
Earlier this month, when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions against any nation continuing to purchase Iranian crude oil, he did not name China. He did not need to. China, the Islamic Republic’s largest oil customer, is squarely in Washington’s crosshairs.
The US has already unveiled new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iranian trade, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong. Just three months after the May summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump appeared to stabilise bilateral trade relations, the fragile calm is being tested again.
So far, China has signalled it will not be coerced. The stand-off sets the stage for what could be the next major rupture in an already fraught relationship.
Washington has not been idle since May. In June, the Pentagon added dozens of companies – including Alibaba, Baidu and BYD – to its list of “Chinese military companies”, a designation that can restrict these companies’ access to US capital and market. In July, it announced a 10-12.5 per cent tariff on goods from 60 economies, including China, following its Section 301 investigation into forced labour.
This was followed by a ban on imports of Chinese robots and power inverters (July) and a 15 per cent tariff on polysilicon (August). The cumulative message is clear: Washington is tightening the screws on multiple fronts, and Iran is merely the latest lever.
Beijing’s response to this onslaught has been deliberate and calibrated. Gone are the days of blanket tariff retaliation. Instead, China has preferred to hold its fire where the cost of escalation outweighs the benefits, striking back with precision when core interests are threatened.

articles.title: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? | John Harris
articles.body:
Apart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.
So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.
One change became clear earlier this year, and now looks like it will be turbocharged. By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts.
These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.
England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”
And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne, Minehead, Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.
Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to a House of Commons library briefing, qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.
A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will include Wiltshire, Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.
When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took its first steps to joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades, finally agreed to become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer government postponed mayoral elections in Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.
And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring the State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news that plans for new, larger police forces are being delayed because their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.
There is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.
Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: ‘Violation of High Court order won't be tolerated’: Agnimitra Paul reacts after FIR against Mamata Banerjee
articles.body:
‘Violation of High Court order won't be tolerated’: Agnimitra Paul reacts after FIR against Mamata Banerjee
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 30, 2026, 17:27 IST

File photo: Bengal minister Agnimitra Paul and Ex-Bengal CM Mamata Banerjee
NEW DELHI: West Bengal minister Agnimitra Paul on Sunday said that any violation of a Calcutta High Court order, irrespective of the person involved, "would not be tolerated", after an FIR was registered against former chief minister Mamata Banerjee over alleged violations during a Trinamool Chhatra Parishad (TMCP) programme in Kolkata.Speaking to news agency ANI, Paul alleged that the previous Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress government had shown disrespect towards the Calcutta High Court and that judges were repeatedly insulted during its tenure."Any violation of the High Court's order, whether by Mamata Banerjee or anyone else, will not be tolerated. The previous government showed disrespect to the High Court; judges were repeatedly insulted... now, such things will not be tolerated," Paul said.
FIR over alleged violation of court order
Banerjee and organisers of the West Bengal Trinamool Chhatra Parishad (WBTMCP) programme have been booked by Hastings Police over the alleged violation of a Calcutta High Court order during the organisation's foundation day programme at Cathedral Road on August 28.According to police, the case was registered at Hastings Police Station on August 28 based on a written complaint submitted by Sub-Inspector Apu Baidya.
The FIR includes Sections 61(2), 223, 125(a), 132 and 285 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), relating to allegations including criminal conspiracy, disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant, acts endangering life or personal safety, assault or criminal force against public servants, and negligent conduct with respect to public ways.Police alleged that Banerjee and the organisers violated an order passed by the Calcutta High Court in connection with WPA No. 21728 of 2026.According to the complaint, the programme was scheduled to be held from 12 noon to 3 pm under the permission and directions referred to in the complaint. Police alleged that the organisers continued the programme beyond the permitted time.
Police allege barricades were breached
The complaint alleged that Banerjee and the organisers provoked supporters during the programme, following which the crowd pushed aside barricades put up by police.Supporters allegedly jostled with police personnel deployed at the venue, creating a chaotic situation, according to the police account. The gathering also allegedly obstructed vehicular movement on one flank of Cathedral Road.The Calcutta High Court had imposed conditions for the programme, with Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya directing on Tuesday that efforts be made to keep attendance within 1,500.The court had also directed police to ensure that law and order was maintained and that vehicular movement on one flank of the road was not affected.
Indranil Khan also attacks Mamata
West Bengal minister Indranil Khan also criticised Banerjee, alleging that she had repeatedly disrespected constitutional institutions and the judiciary."Mamata Banerjee never respected the country's laws or its Constitution. Even while serving as Chief Minister, she made highly objectionable and disrespectful remarks against the Calcutta High Court and its judges. Today, although the people of West Bengal have removed her from the post of Chief Minister and she is no longer even an MLA, she remains unable to shed that mindset," Khan told reporters.
He further alleged that Banerjee had considered herself above the rule of law in the state."She used to consider herself above the rule of law in West Bengal, and that attitude persists. Consequently, attacking the judiciary and violating the law have become habitual for her," he added.Police said the role of all those involved in the alleged violations would be examined during the course of the investigation, news agency PTI reported.

Tejashwi accused the two Union ministers of acting on the “instructions” of RSS.
NEW DELHI: RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday took a jibe at the BJP and RSS, saying, “guḍ khaye, gulgule se parhez”, amid the spat between NDA allies Chirag Paswan and Jitan Ram Manjhi over reservation.The leader of opposition in Bihar assembly also accused the two Union ministers of acting on the “instructions” of the RSS and alleged that the BJP-RSS was “anti-reservation”.He also challenged Chirag and Manjhi to resign from their posts and contest elections from unreserved seats if they opposed reservation.Taking a dig at the two leaders on X, Tejashwi said, “Guḍ khaye, gulgule se parhez!” He alleged that Chirag and Manjhi were speaking in different voices on the issue of sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations while allegedly acting on the directions of the RSS.“Two Union Ministers, Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi and Chirag Paswan, are speaking in opposite directions on the instructions of RSS, diverting attention from the original objective of BJP-RSS to end reservations, and want to gauge the sentiments of reservation supporters,” he said.He alleged that both ministers, who were elected from reserved constituencies, were benefiting from reservation while being part of the BJP-led NDA.
“First and foremost, these ministers, elected from reserved quotas, are sitting in the lap of the Constitution and reservation opponents, enjoying the peak pleasures of power,” Tejashwi said.“If these two have a deep hatred for reservations, let them contest elections from unreserved seats and see their - eyes will open,” he added.Tejashwi also questioned the position of NDA allies in Bihar, including the parties led by Nitish Kumar, Upendra Kushwaha, Chirag Paswan and Jitan Ram Manjhi, on the 65% reservation quota introduced by the state government.“If these parties are pro-reservation, then why don't they get the increased 65% reservation limit in Bihar, raised in our government, included in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution?” he asked.
Chirag-Manjhi lock horns over quota within quotaTejashwi's remarks came a day after differences within the NDA over sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations became public, with Chirag Paswan and Jitan Ram Manjhi taking opposing positions.The row began after Manjhi and his son, Bihar minister Santosh Kumar Suman, supported the idea of sub-categorisation to ensure that the most deprived Dalit communities receive a greater share of reservation benefits.Chirag, who heads the Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), strongly opposed any move to review reservation and demanded that Manjhi and his son resign if they supported such a measure.“The constitutional provision of SC/ST reservation is based on social discrimination and not economic status. If they want to change the Constitution, then debate the issue in Parliament. Those who talk or think about reviewing reservation should first resign, as they actually want to completely end it and reduce its scope,” Chirag said.He also asserted that reservation was in place in the past, remains in place today and would continue in the future.Responding to Chirag's demand, Suman said he was ready to resign, but challenged Chirag to take the first step.“As far as resignations go, we are ready. My younger brother’s party is the bigger one; they have more numbers than us and are politically third-generation too, so let them take the lead. Let him step forward by resigning and we are prepared to resign alongside him,” Suman said.Tejashwi invokes Bhagwat's 2015 remarkTejashwi also targeted RSS chief over his earlier remarks on reviewing reservation, saying, “Mohan Bhagwat had also spoken earlier about reviewing reservations”, adding that Bihar “ne unke kaan pakad kar achhe se uthak-baithak karwa di thi. Ab phir karenge toh Bihari log RSS/BJP ka murga bana dega.”He was referring to Bhagwat's 2015 call for a review of the reservation policy, which became a major political issue during the Bihar assembly election that year.Tejashwi said ending reservation was “a remote possibility” and accused the BJP of testing public sentiment on the issue. “None can put an end to reservation. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat called for a review of reservation in 2015, and the people of Bihar taught him a lesson,” the RJD leader said.
“These people are merely characters. They only want posts. They are greedy for positions, chairs, bungalows and security, but they have left society behind...” he added.The dispute comes amid renewed political debate over SC/ST sub-categorisation after the Supreme Court's August 1, 2024 Constitution Bench judgment held that states can create sub-categories within SC and ST reservations to ensure benefits reach the most disadvantaged communities.The issue has particular significance in Bihar, where Dalit communities are socially and politically diverse. The state government introduced the Mahadalit category in 2007 to identify the most deprived Dalit communities.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. articles.title: ‘Without us, no wheel would turn’: the unsung heroes keeping England’s transport moving
articles.body:
Not many people get to park their car here – bang in the middle of Heathrow airport, on the taxiway just a stretch of grass away from where a line of passenger planes is coming in to land.
It’s close enough to see the shimmering air and smoke as nose tyres hit the tarmac. “An A380 will put down as much rubber as a car’s entire tyre,” Jack Quantick-Thorne says. He knows – part of his job is to ensure the runway team scrapes it off and patches things up overnight. And it is all recycled, he adds.
The airfield operations officer is not in the limelight much, but is one of a host of unsung workers keeping transport moving. And some jobs far from the public eye turn out to be not only essential, but surprisingly challenging.
Jack Quantick-Thorne, airfield operations officer, Heathrow
Passengers might only catch a glimpse of Quantick-Thorne from a window seat on landing, if he grabs the paddles to marshal a plane into the exact designated spot at the stand. “People just think you’re that person with the table tennis bats,” he grimaces slightly, as the Guardian requests a demonstration. “That’s like 5% of my job.”
In fact, most planes are now brought to the stand via laser-guided electronic displays. But human marshalling remains a crucial backup. Brandishing the paddles, Quantick-Thorne beckons in a taxiing British Airways arrival, the pilot peering down from the cockpit and steering 50 tonnes of plane straight towards him. The nosewheel travels bang on the guideline, stopping exactly in position for the airbridge to swing in and allow passengers to disembark.
Nerve-racking? “No. When you’ve got a really big plane, an A380, you need a second marshal right by the wheel to check it’s stopped in the right place,” he says.
Back in the car, the job continues: “I’m patrolling, I’m looking around, scanning everything – is the refueller doing his job properly, has the aircraft got chocks under its wheels?”
That includes monitoring the road system under Heathrow’s airfields, recognising every vehicle and checking any infringement: drivers here can also clock up points on their licence, if he spots them.
Officers also need to look out for wildlife – particularly birds, a serious danger for jet planes (and vice versa). How does he deal with them? “We’ve got methods of dispersal,” says the airfield operations officer.
These, marvellously, turn out to be speakers on the roof of the van, which play a range of bird sounds: “If I saw a flock of starlings, if I played a starling noise, the starling would think, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a predator nearby,’ and they fly off.”
And, he demonstrates, “I’ve got common gull. Black-headed gull. I’ve got a falcon”.
Are there falcons? “No,” he explains patiently. “So you think about it from a bird’s point of view. If there’s a pigeon over there, best play a falcon so it will fly off.”
If he now knows birds, it’s the planes that drew him here. He was previously at Nats, the air traffic control centre in Swanwick, managing the planes, but never up close. There is more to it than the paddles – but, he confesses, he takes every opportunity to use them, and records each plane that he has marshalled, including every aircraft in BA’s short-haul fleet.
Being a pilot is the dream, he admits, but the prohibitive training costs – £100,000 or more – put it out of reach. For an enthusiast, he reckons the job is the next best thing. Last year he had to tow the Concorde that still stands at the edge of the airfield across for an exhibition: “It was the first time one had moved in years – incredible to see in the rear-view mirror.”
Chris Thackaberry, network traffic controller, Transport for London
The day starts in Victoria Station House overlooking the bus terminus, a grand old building that looks considerably less so inside, where Chris’s desk is surrounded by hundreds of cardboard diversion signs.
About 500 of the capital’s 19,000 bus stops are on his patch in Westminster – home to some of Britain’s most congested streets, where dozens of bus routes cross. Roadworks are the bane of the bus and Thackaberry’s job is to keep them moving – armed with a van, pliers and zip ties.
Sometimes he can plan for roadworks months ahead. But other days are less predictable, when life suddenly blocks a route: “It could be a broken-down vehicle or a burst water main, but I’ve had windows falling out of buildings, I’ve had a collapsed horse on a bridge. I had an upside down Lamborghini in Piccadilly … I don’t know if it was sticking to the 20mph limit.”
His incident response van contains an orderly standing desk area and even a printer to rustle up more signs if needed, as well as spill dry sacks, ready to suck up any diesel or oil leaked over the road.
It also has two cylinders affixed to the wall containing “spit kits” – swabs to pick up any saliva aimed at staff, with clear bags to seal, ready to take the evidence to the police. “It’s just part and parcel of when you’re working in London, for anyone in uniform.”
In a sweltering Trafalgar Square, as he hunts in the midst of four lanes of traffic to hitch his cardboard signs to any available piece of spare street furniture, the complexity of the puzzle becomes clearer.
“There’s so many routes go through here, we’re fighting with ourselves for space.”
Sarah, railway signaller, York
Gone are most of the signal boxes of old: these days, Britain’s railway is mostly controlled from one of 12 remote centres. From a windowless room in York, trains right down the East Coast mainline are guided on their way.
“In the old days, it was lever pulling,” says Sarah. “Now it’s a click of the mouse instead. Like a computer game scenario, but it’s real track, real trains, real people. We have to manually click, signal to signal, for every train that comes through our patch.”
Signallers have five screens at eye level showing the railway, and five above with timetables and traffic management information.
“When you first start the job, it feels so far removed. There’s no windows, it’s like a black hole in the middle of the building, but you are signalling trains from York all the way into King’s Cross. I remember thinking: ‘How many hundreds of people are on that train we’re signalling?’”
Anything from a circuit failure to a trespasser to a sick passenger on a train can hold up the lines. “Our job initially in any incident is to make the area safe – that’s first and foremost. And then we look for a workaround, to keep trains moving. The days when there are serious incidents are few and far between. But every day there’s something.”
Jamie *, public service vehicle engineer, Manchester
At Jamie’s bus depot, servicing the Bee Network, the first shift starts at 5am and the last ends at 1am, but engineers might stay through the night with a breakdown.
“In the daytime it’s routine: vehicles are inspected by law on a monthly basis,” he says. “But engineers have bus driving licences too, if a bus was to break down, often we’d take another one out to the driver to keep the service running.”
With city buses that stop and start frequently, there is typically more treatment and maintenance. And newer vehicles don’t necessarily mean less work, he says: “They bring a lot of new issues and we’re constantly learning, going back to college on courses to learn the tech.
“Electric buses haven’t made the job easier – but they and the new diesel engines are clean. Working back in the day, it was a hell of a lot dirtier, especially in depots indoors or undercover,” says the vehicle engineer.
He will check each bus’s brakes, emissions tests and inspect the nuts and bolts everywhere from the underside to the driver’s cab. “We see a lot in the press about the conditions in the cab, but we’re cleaning those buses: it’s like a greenhouse, and the heat from the engines also comes into our workshop.
“Even the drivers don’t understand what engineers do – I always say we are the forgotten people. But without us, no wheel would turn.”
Frankie *, baggage handler, Gatwick
The thing people don’t understand, explains Frankie, is that the placement of bags in the hold is not random. “It’s all done on weight distribution. You have to put baggage where you’re told – it is a very specific job, you do not deviate.”
At many airports, larger aircraft such as long-haul planes are loaded with bags already in large crates, lifted into position by machine. But short-haul flights at Gatwick are loaded manually. “An average bag is about 20kg and the average load is 90 bags off, 90 on, for three or four people. If you do eight turns a day, that’s nearly 30 tonnes your team is lifting. You get fitter – it’s like going to the gym, you end up lifting heavier and heavier bags.”
Passengers who fear for their luggage often make the job harder: “The worst thing is shrink-wrapped bags. It’s slippery, harder to hold on to, and less grip for the belt to pull up. And those straps around bags, they can get jammed in the belts and break them.
“People don’t realise how damaging it can be – and pointless. If you’re on a flight where customs do spot checks, they go for the bags that are wrapped. And there is so much CCTV and security. If I get caught opening a bag, I’d lose my job – why would I risk that?”
There are, says Frankie, more women doing the job now: “It’s getting more female-friendly. A lot of people choose this type of job to get into aviation: they want to be pilots or crew eventually, and just want to be around planes any way they can.”
* Names have been changed

articles.title: Prosecutors consider charges against officers involved in spycops scandal
articles.body:
Prosecutors are examining whether to bring criminal charges against 12 former police officers who were involved in spying on political groups.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) is examining a file of evidence that the officers may have committed wrongdoing while working in controversial undercover operations.
It follows a police investigation into Mark Kennedy, an undercover officer who infiltrated environmental and leftwing groups for six years.
Kennedy is a key figure in the spycops scandal. He deceived a number of women into intimate relationships while concealing from them that he was a police spy. The total number is unknown, but is believed to be in double figures.
Prosecutors are considering whether to authorise charges against the other officers under the offence of misconduct in public office. However, details of the alleged wrongdoing have not been made public.
Kennedy was one of 139 undercover officers who spied on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over more than four decades.
If the CPS decides to launch a prosecution of any of the 12 officers, it would be the first time that any officer involved in the undercover operations, which lasted between 1968 and at least 2010, were criminally charged with any kind of wrongdoing that had not been authorised by their managers.
The spycops scandal has revealed that the undercover officers committed a range of misconduct. These included regularly deceiving women into sexual relationships, lying in court proceedings when they appeared in their fake identities, and stealing the identities of dead children.
Like the other undercover officers, Kennedy adopted a fake identity to infiltrate environmental groups such as Earth First! and Climate Camp between 2003 and 2009. He transformed himself from an ordinary police officer into a long-haired, tattooed protester. He worked for the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, one of two squads that infiltrated undercover officers into political groups.
He had a six-year intimate relationship with a social justice campaigner, known as Lisa Jones. Through her own detective work, she uncovered his real identity in 2010.
This exposure led to the outbreak of the spycops scandal and was the first in a string of revelations, which has over time disclosed the scale of misconduct.
These led to the long-running public inquiry, which has been examining the activities and management of the undercover officers.
It also led to the police setting up a number of their own internal investigations into alleged criminal behaviour by individual officers.
One of these, known as Operation Montrose, examined the conduct of Kennedy and others.
Police have previously said Operation Montrose was examining whether Kennedy had conducted “inappropriate sexual relationships” while undercover.
Initiated in 2015, the investigation has been run under the auspices of the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC).
The NPCC confirmed that it had sent a file of evidence relating to Kennedy and 11 other police officers to the CPS. The nature of the alleged wrongdoing by the other police officers is unclear.
Kennedy had a two-year relationship with Kate Wilson, a campaigner. She won a landmark victory in 2021, when judges in a tribunal decided that police had grossly violated her human rights.
The judges concluded that senior officers in charge of Kennedy “either knew of the relationship, chose not to know of its existence, or were incompetent and negligent in not following up” clear and obvious signs.
Covert surveillance files showed how the police secretly monitored and recorded her personal activities during the relationship. They recorded how Wilson and Kennedy frequently stayed together, visited her parents’ house, and went on holiday.
They chronicled trips the couple made to the cinema, a museum and a concert, as well as a visit to the college where she had studied.
Kennedy’s lawyer said he did not wish to comment.
