articles.title: Career finance official moves into pole position to become Shanghai’s next mayor
articles.body:
Career finance official moves into pole position to become Shanghai’s next mayor
Zhu Zhongming, a former vice-minister for finance, has been appointed to a leading role in the city’s government
Shanghai has named career finance official Zhu Zhongming as the municipal government’s new party chief, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next mayor.
His appointment as secretary of the Shanghai government’s Party Leadership Group was announced on Saturday in an official social media post that said he had chaired a meeting of the body.
Zhu replaces the current mayor, Gong Zheng, in the post. However, the city’s most senior position is that of the secretary of the Shanghai Communist Party committee, which is currently held by Chen Jining.
In China’s party-state system, municipal governments operate under the leadership of the party, which sets the broader political direction while the government handles day-to-day administration.
Zhu’s appointment comes a year ahead of the next national party congress, which is expected to see a major leadership reshuffle.
If Chen is promoted to a more senior role in Beijing, a move that would be in keeping with the precedent set over the past two decades, it would create vacancies at the top of Shanghai’s leadership.
Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he is believed to have crossed paths with Premier Li Qiang during the latter’s spell as governor.

articles.title: Iceland votes against resuming EU accession talks
articles.body:
Iceland votes against resuming EU accession talks
Iceland has narrowly rejected the idea of resuming talks on joining the EU, public broadcaster RUV has reported. Previous negotiations were halted 13 years ago.
The referendum on Saturday saw a high turnout, with more than 225,000 people out of a population of just over 394,000 coming to the polls.
After the ballot count concluded on Sunday, RUV announced that 52.8% said ‘no’ to resuming accession talks, while 47.2% backed the idea.
The ballot asked voters just a single question: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
The country’s capital Reykjavik voted ‘Yes’, while people in rural areas were overwhelmingly against the EU path, underlining a split between the two parts of the country.
Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev has welcomed the outcome of the referendum, saying in a post on X that “Iceland knows how to play great football and how to reject the failing EU’s migrants, bureaucrats, and warmongering.”
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but moved it to an earlier date due to geopolitical tensions, including US President Donald Trump’s threats to annex neighboring Greenland, which is an autonomous territory of Denmark.
In January, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Iceland, Billy Long, suggested that country could become the “52nd state” of the US, with himself as governor. However, he later apologized and called it a joke.
Before the vote, Frostadottir’s allies portrayed the EU as additional protection for the country, while Euroskeptics argued that Brussels itself was becoming increasingly militarized and confrontational. Iceland is already a founding NATO member and maintains extensive military ties with Washington.
Supporters of restarting the talks also argued that closer EU integration could bring greater economic and currency stability, while giving the country more influence over rules it already adopts through the European Economic Area.
Opponents focused heavily on sovereignty, agriculture, and above all, Iceland’s fishing grounds, warning that membership could subject the strategically vital industry to the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy.
The leader of the Heimssyn eurosceptic movement, Haraldur Olafsson, told Ruptly before the referendum that Brussels was “definitely a greater threat to the sovereignty of Iceland than any other superpower in the world.”
The US only asks for an area for a military base in the country and a government that “isn’t very hostile” to Washington, while the EU “wants to govern the county. They want to set the law,” he explained.

articles.title: Nut consumption is associated with sharper thinking skills and post-stroke brain health markers
articles.body:
People who eat more nuts tend to score higher on tests of thinking and memory, especially if they have generally poor diets or exercise habits. Among individuals who have experienced a stroke, eating nuts is linked to higher levels of a protein that helps grow new blood vessels. These findings, published in Food & Function, provide evidence that even small dietary additions might offer benefits for brain health.
A person’s ability to manage everyday life depends heavily on maintaining mental sharpness as they age. A 2026 review highlighted that cardiovascular risk factors and diet in middle age interact to shape the long-term health of the brain, either protecting it or accelerating its decline over a lifespan. Strokes are especially disruptive, causing direct damage to brain tissue and increasing the risk of memory problems and dementia. Because medical treatments for dementia remain limited, many experts are looking at preventative measures like diet.
Healthy eating patterns, such as the Mediterranean diet, tend to feature nutrient-rich foods that help protect blood vessels and reduce inflammation. Nuts are a core part of these dietary patterns. They contain healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals that promote cardiovascular health, but their specific role in maintaining cognitive function is still being mapped out.
“Nuts are widely recommended as part of a healthy diet and have known benefits for heart and metabolic health, but evidence for their benefits to cognitive health is inconsistent,” said co-authors Barbara R. Cardoso, a senior lecturer at Monash University, and Sasan Amanat, a PhD student. “Further, we are particularly interested in stroke survivors, a group at higher risk of cognitive decline that has been relatively understudied in nutrition research.”
To explore these questions, the researchers utilized data from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort, a large-scale project that began tracking Massachusetts residents in the 1970s. The research focused on 1,771 participants with an average age of 61 who completed dietary surveys and underwent tests of their thinking skills. Of this group, 1,742 participants had no history of stroke, while 29 were stroke survivors.
Participants reported their food intake over the past year using detailed questionnaires, allowing the team to estimate their average daily nut consumption. On average, the stroke-free participants ate about 1.3 grams of nuts per day, a very low amount compared to standard dietary guidelines. The participants also completed neuropsychological tests measuring their processing speed, visual memory, verbal memory, and reasoning. These test results were combined into a single score for general cognitive function.
To look inside the brain, the researchers used magnetic resonance imaging to measure the volume of total brain tissue and the volume of the hippocampus, a region essential for memory. They also took blood samples to measure two proteins required for the development and maintenance of the nervous system. One was brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which helps nerves survive, and the other was vascular endothelial growth factor, which stimulates the formation of new blood vessels. The team accounted for variables such as age, sex, education, smoking status, overall diet quality, and physical activity.
Among the participants without a history of stroke, consuming more nuts was associated with higher overall cognitive scores. When the researchers grouped people by their lifestyle habits, they found that this benefit was most pronounced in individuals who engaged in the least physical activity and had the lowest overall diet quality. In those groups, small increases in nut intake translated to better memory and thinking scores.
“Our findings add to growing evidence that including a handful of nuts in the diet may support cognitive health,” the researchers told PsyPost. “Swapping less healthy snacks for nuts could be especially helpful for people who do not eat a balanced diet or who are not very physically active. Brain health is often discussed in terms of complex treatments or interventions, but our research highlights the potential importance of everyday dietary choices. Nuts are widely available and can easily replace discretionary foods in many dietary patterns.”
The brain scan results offered a different pattern. Eating more nuts was associated with a larger total brain volume, but only among participants who were highly physically active. In the general stroke-free group, nut consumption was not linked to the levels of the brain health proteins in the blood.
For the small group of stroke survivors, nut intake did not show an association with memory and thinking scores. Higher nut consumption did correspond to elevated levels of vascular endothelial growth factor in the blood, which could indicate a better environment for repairing blood vessels after a stroke.
“We were surprised to see that nut intake was associated with vascular endothelial growth factor in stroke survivors,” the researchers explained. “Although our findings are limited by the small number of participants and therefore need confirmation in larger studies, they shed light on a possible mechanism by which a particular food may help stroke survivors recover.”
Over a ten-year follow-up period, the researchers also tracked the incidence of new strokes and dementia cases among the stroke-free participants. Out of 1,742 people, they identified 49 new strokes and 61 new dementia cases, finding no statistical relationship between the amount of nuts eaten and the likelihood of developing these conditions.
The cognitive findings are consistent with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that regular nut consumption was associated with a 12 percent reduced risk of dementia. The current study, which assessed cognitive test scores and brain health markers rather than clinical dementia incidence over a longer period, similarly found cognitive benefits linked to nut consumption.
The results also align with a 2025 study indicating that eating 60 grams of peanuts daily improved verbal memory and brain blood flow. Although the new study examined habitual nut consumption across a large population rather than a controlled daily peanut intervention, it similarly suggests a benefit for brain health. Another 2026 study reported improved cognitive processing speed following daily almond consumption in adults with prediabetes. The current research extends this concept by looking at general cognition across a broader community group.
The findings provide a helpful perspective on diet, but there are several reasons to interpret them cautiously. “One important limitation is that this study can only show a link between nut consumption and better brain health, not prove that one causes the other,” the researchers noted. “In other words, while people who ate more nuts tended to have better cognitive function, the research does not show that eating nuts directly prevents memory loss or cognitive decline.”
Additionally, the overall intake of nuts in the studied population was extremely low, with only a tiny fraction of people meeting standard dietary guidelines of 20 grams per day. Exploring similar questions in populations that eat a wider variety and larger quantity of nuts could clarify the exact amounts needed to protect brain function as people age.
“We are particularly interested in stroke survivors because they face an increased risk of cognitive decline, yet remain underrepresented in nutrition research,” the researchers said. “Our next goal is to better understand how dietary factors, including nut consumption, may support recovery, rehabilitation, and long-term brain health after stroke.”
The study, “Nut consumption, cognitive function and brain health markers in individuals with and without stroke: cross-sectional and longitudinal findings from the Framingham heart study,” was authored by Sasan Amanat, Aimee L. Dordevic, Matthew P. Pase, and Barbara R. Cardoso.

articles.title: Ukrainian interceptor drones powerless against new Russian jet-powered UAVs — newspaper
articles.body:
BERLIN, August 30. /TASS/. Ukrainian interceptor drones are unable to shoot down Russian jet-powered UAVs, Welt TV correspondent Christoph Wanner stated.
"These Russian jet-powered drones already pose a huge threat to Ukraine. They are having enormous difficulty shooting down these aircraft," the expert noted. First and foremost, in his opinion, this is because "Ukrainian interceptor drones are, at the moment, at least virtually powerless against these new high-speed Russian kamikaze UAVs."
According to the journalist, Ukraine "has not yet kept pace with the development of these technologies for its own interceptor drones," and "the problems are now evident." Wanner noted that Ukrainian interceptors were designed to counter older Russian drones. "However, the Russians subsequently modernized their drones and are now using precisely these jet-powered drones," he stressed, adding that "other developments are on the way.".

articles.title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?
articles.body:
The UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse.
In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle.
What the government needs is big, innovative ideas. We should look to history for inspiration, while also absorbing the lessons of past mistakes.
How about national service – but instead of entering the military, recruits are pledged to the NHS? Eye-catching, but ultimately not right, at least not in that form. Forcing young people to do work they’d prefer not to, when there isn’t even an enemy at the gates, will only lead to bad results. Indeed, the army has already learned this: compulsory recruits in the postwar period were typically unmotivated and incompetent; a drag rather than a boost to the military’s performance.
But that’s a crude precedent. We can take more relevant inspiration from elsewhere. For example, young men in Austria who do not wish to serve in the military can instead opt for health or social care work; many end up driving ambulances. The trade-off is that they do nine months instead of six. In Norway, conscientious objectors were, until 2012, able to perform “civilian national service”, working in community settings such as primary schools or nursing homes, and accruing points towards university entry for doing so.
Thinking along similar lines, how about this? The government offers recent school leavers a deal: 50% off their total university fees if they first spend a year volunteering in social care. (You could even up the ante: 100% off if they commit to two years; full back pay with a bonus if they stay in the profession.)
There are many reasons to take this proposal seriously. First, it is not just social care that is in crisis. University funding is, too. Right now, UK universities are panicking because student enrolment fees no longer keep them in the black. But at the same time, undergraduates are being presented with eye-watering loan bills and interest rates at levels that make capital repayment much harder. We are rapidly approaching a cliff edge. The government is going to have to fix the system one way or the other. Why not do something innovative and radical at the same time?
The overall maths might work surprisingly well. If uptake is sufficiently high, the state gets an enormous amount of free (in the short term) labour to offset the costs of lost loan revenue. If that sounds exploitative, remember that it would be in the interests of young people themselves (in the longer term) because they would leave university with a heck of a lot less debt.
But the upsides go beyond just money. At the moment, unscrupulous agencies too often rely on low-paid migrant labour, ignoring the linguistic and caring skills required do a safe and competent job. A scheme like this would open up a new pool for recruitment – of eager-to-learn young people at the start of their careers.
Of course, they would have to undergo proper training and would only get the discount if they complete the programme to a certified high level. Along the way, some would discover that care work can be deeply rewarding; that the current stigmatisation of this kind of employment just doesn’t tally with reality.
I know, because since I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in care. I am lucky to be with a very good agency, which only employs highly competent and conscientious staff (from all over the world). I have seen up close just how rewarding and dignified care work can be. Sure, there are some icky parts to looking after a man who can’t go to the toilet by himself. But all my care workers take real pride in helping me live as close to a normal life as possible. Of course, they’re not on footballers’ wages. But they get a very visible amount of life satisfaction from helping me find mine.
One of the most interesting care workers I’ve met was covering holiday earlier in the summer. Originally from Ireland, she had just finished a two-year master’s degree at King’s College London (by coincidence where I teach, in a different department). She is now a qualified dietitian, who in future will be working in hospitals. But until she makes that transition she is spending a year with my spinal agency, after having been employed as a care worker in Ireland for two years prior to her degree. It’s a job she finds deeply rewarding.
I am confident that if we incentivised UK students to try social care before university, many would consider rejoining once they had graduated. This would help to reduce wider stigma around care work as the preserve of poor, often vulnerable migrant workers, assumed to be doing it only because no one else will.
Look, I’m neither a government accountant nor a policy expert. Perhaps when we’ve crunched the numbers, it just doesn’t work. But from where I’m sitting this has the potential to be a win-win of the sort that could define the Burnham administration. All the scheme needs is a name, and there’s an obvious one for the taking: “Care First”.
Dr Paul Sagar is a reader in political theory at King’s College London.

The Courage to Care: Nurses, Families and Hope by Christie Watson (Vintage, £10.99)
Who Cares by Emily Kenway (Headline, £12.99)

articles.title: ‘Eagles’ Castle’ photo exhibition brings Alamut heritage to Tehran Metro
articles.body:
‘Eagles’ Castle’ photo exhibition brings Alamut heritage to Tehran Metro
TEHRAN – A photo exhibition showcasing the historic and architectural features of Alamut and Lambsar castles has opened at Tehran’s Mirdamad Metro Station, following the inscription of Alamut Castle and Related Fortifications on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
Titled “Eagles’ Castle,” the exhibition features 20 selected photographs capturing the castles and their surrounding landscapes from various ground and aerial perspectives. The images highlight the historical, architectural and natural features of the fortifications through the lenses of news and media photographers.
The exhibition was organized by the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts in cooperation with Tehran Urban and Suburban Railway Operation Company. It also coincides with the commemoration of Qazvin Day and aims to celebrate the UNESCO inscription of Alamut Castle and Related Fortifications.
According to organizers, the choice of a busy metro station as the venue reflects an effort to take cultural heritage beyond specialized venues such as museums and galleries and bring it into the daily lives of Tehran residents and commuters.
The exhibition is set to move to the other designated stations in the coming days, allowing passengers and residents to view the photographs as part of their daily journeys.
The Alamut fortifications are particularly significant for their strategic locations in a mountainous landscape, where natural topography was incorporated into defensive planning. Their inscription on the World Heritage List has brought renewed international attention to the historical landscape of the Alamut region.
The listed sites include Alamut Castle, Lambsar, Navizarshah, Shams-Kelaye, Qostinlar, Shirkuh and Ilan. Together, they formed an interconnected defensive and administrative system between the 11th and 13th centuries.
AM

articles.title: UK seeks £37m support deal for helicopter forces
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence is preparing a contract worth an estimated £37 million to provide additional engineering, logistics and support personnel for the UK’s Support Helicopter Force and Commando Helicopter Force at RAF Odiham, RAF Benson and RNAS Yeovilton, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The pipeline notice published on 28 August sets out an enduring requirement for contracted personnel across aviation engineering, logistics information systems, airworthiness records, supply and other enabling functions where the MOD says military capacity is constrained.
The planned contract is expected to run from 1 November 2027 until 31 October 2032, with an option to extend the arrangement for a further two years to October 2034. Its estimated value is £37 million excluding VAT, or £44.4 million including VAT.
The MOD intends to use a competitive flexible procedure, with publication of the formal tender notice currently expected on 1 December 2026.
The requirement is explicitly linked to pressure on the Service workforce across engineering and logistics functions. The procurement notice states: “There is an enduring requirement for contracted labour and personnel support across aviation engineering, logistics information systems, airworthiness records, supply and enabling functions at RAF Odiham, RAF Benson and RNAS Yeovilton.”
It adds that the contractor will be required to provide suitably qualified and experienced personnel to supplement Service personnel where military capacity is constrained.
The contract is being structured around outputs rather than a fixed number of posts. The MOD says workforce gap information may be used to guide priorities, but the figures will not amount to a guaranteed staffing requirement or workload for the successful supplier.
According to the notice: “This is an output-based personnel support requirement; it does not prescribe fixed posts or transfer the Authority’s responsibility for directing and assuring Defence outputs.”
The work will support both the Support Helicopter Force and Commando Helicopter Force, covering aircraft availability, maintenance throughput, logistics resilience, airworthiness assurance and the wider generation of operational capability.
The Support Helicopter Force includes the RAF’s heavy and medium battlefield lift capability, centred on aircraft operating from bases including RAF Odiham and RAF Benson. The Commando Helicopter Force, based at RNAS Yeovilton, provides aviation support to the Royal Marines and wider littoral operations.
The MOD says the planned contractor support will help it move scarce engineering and logistics resources between requirements as flying programmes, maintenance activity and readiness demands change.
The notice states: “Support shall remain responsive to flying programme requirements, maintenance activity, emergent tasking, readiness cycles, future capability transition and changes in workload across output groups, functions, locations and time.”
No fixed quantity of work is being guaranteed under the proposed arrangement. Historic workload figures and planning assumptions will instead be used as guidance while the contractor responds to changing requirements across the three sites.
The MOD makes that point explicitly in the notice, stating: “The Authority does not guarantee a fixed volume of tasking. Activity assumptions, historic data and annexed output schedules are indicative and shall not be interpreted as guaranteed workload, fixed workforce demand or a prescriptive staffing schedule.”
The procurement covers engineering support services, helicopter repair and maintenance support and wider air transport support services. The notice also identifies the competition as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises and voluntary, community and social enterprises.

articles.title: China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation enters golden period: Xi
articles.body:
President Xi Jinping on Sunday said that cooperation between China and Kyrgyzstan has ushered in a golden period of rapid development,  as he landed in Bishkek for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 and a state visit to the country.
Upon arrival, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and his wife welcomed Xi and First Lady, Peng Liyuan, at the Manas International Airport.
In a written speech, Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes to Japarov and the people of Kyrgyzstan on behalf of the Chinese government and people.
Noting that the two places share a time-honoured traditional friendship, Xi said that the majestic Tianshan Mountains stand as witnesses to the millennia of friendly exchanges between their peoples.
Over the 34 years since the establishment of diplomatic relations, the China-Kyrgyzstan relationship has withstood the test of a changing international landscape, maintained sound and stable development throughout, and reached the high level of a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.
In recent years, bilateral trade volume and people-to-people exchanges have reached new highs, Xi said, noting that major projects including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway have been successfully implemented, and the tangible results of mutually beneficial cooperation have benefited the two peoples.
Xi said that during the visit, he will have in-depth exchanges of views with Japarov on China-Kyrgyzstan relations, cooperation in various fields between the two countries, and international and regional issues of common concern, and draw a new blueprint for building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future.
"I look forward to attending the SCO Bishkek Summit, working with all parties to revisit the 25-year development experience of the SCO, jointly discuss cooperation plans, create the future of the organisation, and promote the continuous new development of the organisation," Xi said. (Xinhua)

articles.title: Train drivers secure 3.6% pay rise after threat of strikes on busy UK routes
articles.body:
Train drivers have secured a significant pay rise after the threat of strike action was floated on busy routes across the UK, including on the busy London-Manchester line.
The deal, which was agreed on Saturday between Avanti West Coast and the Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen (Aslef) union, is the first to be approved by Andy Burnham in his premiership.
As well as the London-Manchester line – likely to see increased ministerial traffic after the establishment of the No 10 North office – the company also operates services to other big British cities such as Birmingham, Glasgow and Liverpool.
Coming after Aslef announced plans in June to ballot members about possible strike action over pay, the deal – first reported by the Sunday Times – will be seen as a victory for the union. It includes a 3.6% pay rise for drivers, 0.7 percentage points higher than the latest inflation rate, as well as time and a half pay for working Sundays, and £720 if drivers work a fifth day in the week.
Avanti is to be renationalised under the Labour government by spring 2027, with all rail companies due to be under government control by the end of that year. The operator, which is seen as having the worst punctuality rating for any major rail company in the UK, based on figures from the Office of Rail and Road, has cut multiple services in the past year, including the 7am train between Manchester and London, which it cut and brought back in the space of a few days after public scrutiny.
The government said it had “prioritised resolving the rail union disputes, improving services for passengers and saving hundreds of millions in lost revenue to ease the burden on taxpayers”.
But the shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, said the government was “totally capitulating to their union paymasters” and that “taxpayers are being asked to stump up millions simply to save Burnham’s blushes”.
An Aslef spokesperson said on Saturday: “Our job is to enhance our members’ terms and conditions and this deal, struck with Avanti West Coast and approved by the DFTO (Department for Transport Operator), has been accepted.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are pleased to see Avanti West Coast work with Aslef to enable a fair and affordable settlement to keep Britain’s railways moving and prevent disruption for passengers.”

articles.title: Meet the gen Zers finding job opportunities teaching English abroad
articles.body:
A year ago, Arianna Marie, 25, was struggling to control the students in her Florida elementary school classroom.
She was living with her parents to save on rent and quickly feeling her passion for teaching dry up, even though it was her first job since graduation.
“I was extremely burnt out,” Marie said. “We had a teacher shortage, so all of my classes were overcrowded.”
When her district wanted to transfer her to a new school, she looked for opportunities abroad. Through an English-language teaching job in South Korea, Marie is now living in Daegu, a city in the south-eastern part of the country, with enough pay and benefits that she can save and travel.
The fact that it’s the home to K-pop and K-dramas doesn’t hurt – and in a striking shift, she’s rediscovered her love for the job. “I never have to crack down on behavior issues, and both students and teachers respect me so much,” Marie said. “I actually get to focus solely on teaching.”
Marie is part of a program by the South Korean government that is placing native English speakers with a college degree and Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) certificates with local public schools, as it increases spending on education. Benefits include free housing, flight reimbursements, healthcare and monthly salaries starting at about $1,400.
Graduating with a college degree in the US no longer comes with the stability it once guaranteed. Since the Covid pandemic, the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has been higher than the overall unemployment rate.
For those who have a job, earnings have been rising slower than the pace of inflation. New entrants in US public service jobs like teaching are increasingly leaving the profession, citing low pay and high stress.
Other countries, including Japan and Taiwan, are similarly investing in full-time English-language teachers, attracting young workers with benefits they would be hard-pressed to find in their home countries.
Gen Z is spreading the word. Some English-language teachers have garnered thousands of followers on TikTok and Instagram, showing audiences their lives abroad. Marie has been keeping track of her travels, and documenting some of her classroom experiences, on her Instagram account.
The TEFL Institute, which issues TEFL certification courses that accredit English-language teachers, notes that the English-language teaching market was valued at $95bn in 2026, with more than 2m TEFL jobs available worldwide. The market is expected to reach $181bn by 2034, and the Asia-Pacific region is growing the fastest.
As the US federal government has gutted the Department of Education, American public school teachers, who are overwhelmingly female, are especially feeling the pull to overseas jobs.
But the phenomenon isn’t exclusive to Americans, or teachers. Zwiwe Dlamini, 28, was spiraling into a deep depression working as an administrative assistant in Durban, South Africa.
“I’ve always been behind the desk, gathering minutes, gathering meetings, working for CEOs and it was just extremely draining,” Dlamini said.
Though she knew that finding a better job at home would be difficult – the youth unemployment rate in South Africa is notoriously high, at almost 70% – Dlamini still quit her job. After six months of job searching, she knew she would have to look elsewhere.
After she applied to the same program as Marie, she ended up in Incheon, the north-west South Korean city, as an English-language teacher. The free housing and low monthly expenses have allowed her to start paying off her debt while having enough savings to travel and plan for a master’s degree.
“One year ago, [I] could not have imagined the position I am in today,” Dlamini said. “I couldn’t afford food and had [accumulated] debt, so paying it off now and still [experiencing] life to the fullest – I am actually so grateful.”
John Bentley, co-founder of the International TEFL Academy, which offers TEFL certification courses, noted that interest in teaching English abroad particularly soared after the 2024 presidential election.
“With a difficult political and economic situation, we see gen Z turning to TEFL,” he said. “A lot of people go with the intention of staying for just one year. What happens is they fall in love with the country or experience and stay three [or] four years, or even much longer.”
This tracks with a broader trend of Americans who increasingly say that they want to migrate. Last year, a Gallup poll found that 40% of US women said they would move abroad if given the chance.
Marie said her South Korean classroom, which she shares with another teacher, is worlds apart from her former classroom in Florida, where she would handle more than 20 kids on her own.
“We always say that teaching is extremely undervalued in the US, but here you can tell how much they do value it,” she said. “The students are more receptive when I correct them and have so much respect for me as a teacher.”

articles.title: Japanese city pop legend Onuki Taeko makes Taiwan debut
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Japanese City Pop pioneer Onuki Taeko made her Taiwan debut Sunday, performing on the closing night of the Jam Jam Asia music festival at the Taipei Music Center.
Onuki, who has been active in music for more than five decades, reflected on her career during the performance and became emotional as she thanked fans for their continued support. She said she had considered whether to continue performing, but the unwavering support of her fans had allowed her to keep singing, according to MNews.
Onuki has expanded her overseas performances in recent years, including appearances in Los Angeles and South Korea. For her first JJA performance, she selected songs that had proved popular with audiences during her overseas performances.
“I’m really happy to meet everyone,” she told the audience before leaving the stage. She also reminded fans to “stay healthy” and thanked them again for their support.
Onuki's appearance was one of the highlights of JJA, which brought more than 80 Taiwanese and international acts to seven stages at the Taipei Music Center on Aug. 29-30. The lineup included Accusefive, Yang Nai-wen (楊乃文), LINION, Asian Dub Foundation, Le Petit Soldat, and DJ Krush, among others, per a press release.
Born in Tokyo in 1953, Onuki formed Sugar Babe with Tatsuro Yamashita and other musicians in 1973. The group released the album “SONGS” in 1975 before disbanding in 1976, when Onuki launched her solo career with “Grey Skies.” She has released 27 original albums.
Her music has incorporated pop, electronic, and Brazilian influences, as well as acoustic and orchestral arrangements. She also collaborated with Sakamoto Ryuichi on the album “UTAU.” Her music production for the 1997 film “Tokyo Biyori” won the Japan Academy Film Prize for Best Music.
Onuki's earlier recordings have gained a new international audience amid the global resurgence of City Pop. Her 1977 album “SUNSHOWER,” in particular, has been rediscovered by younger listeners and reissued on vinyl.
JJA was held as part of the Taipei Music Expo, which ran from Thursday to Sunday at the Taipei Music Center. TMEX focused this year on technology and sustainability and included exhibitions, international forums, industry matchmaking, and performances.
Organizers said TMEX brought together more than 60 international and domestic music brands and industry organizations, along with more than 100 international industry professionals and creators, to strengthen connections between Taiwan's music industry and overseas markets.

articles.title: ‘Pakistan's port capacity, an advantage for Iran's trade with East Asia’

‘Pakistan's port capacity, an advantage for Iran's trade with East Asia’
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO) described the visit of a Pakistani delegation to Iran—aimed at holding a bilateral meeting and following up on the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee—as the beginning of a brilliant era in the development of economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, and emphasized the need for a long-term perspective on Tehran-Islamabad relations.
According to the TPO Public Relations Department, a bilateral meeting to follow up on the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee was held with the delegation from Pakistan's Ministry of Maritime Affairs at the Isfahan Hall of the Tehran Permanent International Fairgrounds. The meeting was attended by Mohammad-Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of the Trade Promotion Organization, along with TPO deputies and managers, as well as Shahid Ahmed, Chairman of the Karachi Port Trust, and a number of high-ranking representatives from Pakistan's Ministry of Maritime Affairs.
At the start of the meeting, Dehghan Dehnavi emphasized the need to chart a long-term vision for Iran-Pakistan trade, stating: "This meeting should go beyond technical and short-term issues and pursue all matters with a long-term horizon, keeping in view the 10-billion-dollar trade target agreed upon by the leaders of the two countries."
The Head of TPO stressed the necessity of developing shipping lines and land transport between the two countries and said: "In the past, Pakistani goods were transported to Iran through third countries. In line with the long-term vision, direct routes between the two countries should be established and strengthened."
Dehghan Dehnavi spoke of Iran's willingness to diversify its foreign trade routes and make greater use of Pakistan's capacity, and clarified: "Achieving this goal requires the development of cooperation in transport infrastructure and ports."
He also referred to Iran's considerable volume of trade with East Asia, particularly China, and said: "Pakistan's port capacity and transport routes can be utilized to transfer a portion of these goods to Iran via sea and land routes."
Dehghan Dehnavi announced the readiness of the Trade Promotion Organization to reach agreements and negotiate with the Pakistani side, adding: "We are striving to establish a long-term and sustainable trade relationship between the two countries."
The Head of TPO concluded by recalling that the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee—held in Islamabad with the presence of the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade—can pave the way for the development of trade cooperation between the two countries.
Also during the meeting, Shahid Ahmed, head of the Pakistani delegation and Chairman of the Karachi Port Trust, emphasized the need to strengthen cooperation between the two countries in the field of transport and maritime trade, and declared the Pakistani side's readiness to cooperate with Iran in facilitating and expanding trade exchanges.
It is worth noting that at this meeting, Iranian private sector activists also put forward their views and proposals for developing and facilitating trade and economic cooperation between the two countries.

articles.title: Emotional infidelity is linked to a surprising mix of dark and light personality traits
articles.body:
A recent study indicates that the tendency to become emotionally and mentally preoccupied with someone outside of a romantic relationship is driven by a complex mix of personality traits and relationship dynamics. The research suggests that this type of infidelity is not just tied to dark or impulsive personality traits, but also to generally positive characteristics like emotional sensitivity. The findings were published in Psychological Reports.
Infidelity is a common issue in romantic relationships, often leading to emotional distress and couples therapy. Historically, people have defined infidelity through physical acts, but modern perspectives recognize that subtle psychological behaviors also play a major role in relationship disengagement. One such phenomenon is extradyadic infatuation. This term describes a state where a person maintains their primary relationship but becomes cognitively, emotionally, and motivationally preoccupied with someone else.
To better grasp why some people develop these alternative attractions, scientists look at individual personality differences and relationship quality. For instance, a 2019 systematic review found that a combination of personal background and relationship dynamics strongly influences whether someone engages in infidelity.
Personality traits are often categorized into broad frameworks to understand interpersonal behavior. The Dark Triad consists of Machiavellianism (a tendency toward manipulation and emotional detachment), narcissism (an inflated sense of importance), and psychopathy (impulsivity and a lack of empathy). On the other hand, the Light Triad focuses on prosocial human characteristics. Introduced in a 2019 study, the Light Triad framework includes Kantianism (treating people as ends rather than means), humanism (valuing the dignity of individuals), and faith in humanity (believing in human goodness).
Another relevant trait is sociosexuality, which describes a person’s willingness to engage in casual sex without emotional commitment. Research, such as a 2021 study of young adults, indicates that dark personality traits and an openness to casual sex frequently interact to influence how people pursue short-term romantic encounters. The authors of the new study aimed to see how this blend of dark traits, light traits, sociosexuality, and relationship satisfaction predicts the specific experience of extradyadic infatuation.
“What initially caught our attention was the idea that infidelity is not always as straightforward as we tend to think,” said study author Teodora-Elena Huțanu, a PhD student at the Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences at Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași in Romania. “Rather than viewing infidelity simply as a matter of ‘good’ versus ‘bad’ people, we wanted to explore a more nuanced picture that considers Dark and Light Triad personality traits, sociosexuality, and relationship quality.”
The research involved a sample of 303 Romanian adults. Participants were between 19 and 64 years old and were currently in a committed romantic relationship. A key requirement for participation was that respondents had to report liking or feeling attracted to someone they knew personally, other than their current partner. Most of the participants were women, and the majority were married or in long-term relationships.
The respondents completed several questionnaires. They answered items assessing their Dark Triad and Light Triad traits. They also completed measures of their sociosexuality, rating their attitudes, behaviors, and desires regarding uncommitted sex. Finally, participants rated their current relationship satisfaction and the intensity of their extradyadic infatuation, which included their thoughts, emotions, and desires regarding their outside attraction.
In their initial analysis, the scientists found that people scoring higher on any of the Light Triad traits tended to report less extradyadic infatuation. Those scoring higher on Dark Triad traits, sociosexuality, or who had lower relationship satisfaction tended to report higher levels of infatuation.
When the researchers analyzed all these factors together to see which ones independently predicted extradyadic infatuation, a more complicated picture emerged. High psychopathy, high sociosexuality, and low relationship satisfaction reliably predicted greater preoccupation with an outside person. A lack of faith in humanity also predicted higher infatuation, suggesting that people with cynical views about others might invest less in their primary relationship and look elsewhere.
Interestingly, two traits behaved differently than expected once other variables were accounted for. Humanism, which initially seemed protective, became a positive predictor of infatuation. The researchers suggest that the emotional sensitivity and openness characteristic of humanism might make people more receptive to forming deep, emotionally meaningful connections with alternative partners.
In contrast, Machiavellianism became a negative predictor in the final analysis. Because extradyadic infatuation requires sustained emotional and cognitive energy, people high in Machiavellianism might avoid such intense attachments due to their preference for strategic, detached interactions. Narcissism and Kantianism did not emerge as statistically significant predictors in the final model.
“What surprised us most was that, even when looking at extradyadic infatuation as a more cognitive, emotional, and motivational form of infidelity, rather than simply as a behavioral transgression, some less adaptive psychological characteristics still remained relevant,” Huțanu explained. “At the same time, the unexpected changes in direction for Machiavellianism and Humanism were also particularly informative.”
“Our findings showed that both Dark and Light Triad traits contributed to its prediction, but in different directions,” Huțanu noted. “This is particularly interesting because it suggests that extradyadic infatuation cannot simply be understood as the result of being manipulative, impulsive, or otherwise ‘dark’.”
“Some of the characteristics involved may also reflect greater emotional receptivity and openness to meaningful interpersonal connections,” she added. “So, rather than asking whether someone who experiences extradyadic infatuation is simply a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ person, we may need to look at what kind of psychological and relational processes are making another person emotionally salient in the first place.”
The study has a few limitations to consider. The sample consisted mostly of women, which might restrict how well the results apply to men. Additionally, the researchers did not account for different relationship agreements, such as whether participants were in strictly monogamous partnerships or consensually non-monogamous arrangements. Open relationship structures might alter how traits like sociosexuality interact with relationship satisfaction.
“An important caveat is that we assessed extradyadic infatuation rather than actual infidelity behavior; therefore, we cannot determine whether participants acted sexually or otherwise on their attraction to an extradyadic person,” Huțanu said. “In addition, extradyadic infatuation may partly reflect an idealized or imagined representation of the other person, particularly when the actual interpersonal bond is limited.”
Because the data was collected at a single point in time, the findings cannot determine whether these personality traits cause infatuation, or if they simply tend to co-occur. “In my future research I would like to clarify how these cognitions and emotions unfold over time and whether extradyadic infatuation ultimately translates into behavioral infidelity or sustained extradyadic relationships,” Huțanu explained. “I am quite confident that this research is only the beginning of a broader effort to highlight more nuanced and comprehensive perspectives on infidelity, which may be psychologically more complex than its behavioral expression suggests.”
The study, “Personality, Relationship Quality, and Infidelity: Extradyadic Infatuation as Predicted by Dark and Light Triad Traits, Sociosexuality and Relationship Satisfaction,” was authored by Teodora-Elena Huțanu and Andrei Corneliu Holman.

articles.title: Tzu Chi provides medical aid, disaster relief in flood-hit Nepal
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Tzu Chi Foundation is providing emergency medical assistance and disaster relief in Nepal following catastrophic flash floods triggered by a glacier collapse.
The foundation’s Nepal chapter has sent medical personnel and volunteers to affected areas and delivered emergency supplies, including protective equipment for workers handling victims’ remains, per CNA.
Nepal’s death toll from the Aug. 26 disaster reached 734 on Sunday, while 2,498 people remained missing, according to the country’s latest government figures. The flooding and landslides struck northern Nepal and areas across the border in China’s Tibet region.
Tzu Chi delivered 120 sets of protective clothing, face masks, and medical gloves to assist military, police, and healthcare personnel recovering bodies. The foundation is also coordinating additional supplies through its Singapore chapter.
An advance Tzu Chi team reported that more than 100 households in a village in Galchhi, Dhading District, lacked basic necessities. Volunteers delivered blankets, bottled water, and dry food to the affected residents.
A Tzu Chi medical team made up of local medical personnel and volunteers traveled to Dhading District, about 87 kilometers west of Kathmandu, to provide assistance and assess medical needs. The foundation has also mobilized local volunteers to purchase rice, beans, cooking utensils, and other necessities in Kathmandu for delivery to affected communities, per CNA.
Tzu Chi teams are also assisting hospitals in Chitwan District, where large numbers of bodies have been recovered following the disaster. The foundation said local volunteers reported shortages of cold-storage facilities and protective equipment needed for handling remains.
Tzu Chi said its headquarters in Taiwan has prepared additional relief supplies and is ready to dispatch aid as transportation conditions allow. Its Nepal teams are continuing to assess needs in affected communities and hospitals.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau votes to reshape presidency
articles.body:
Guinea-Bissau votes to reshape presidency
August 30, 2026
Guinea-Bissau voted on Sunday in a referendum on whether to give the president new powers as the country prepares to transition from military to democratic rule.
The tiny West African nation of around 2.2 million people has been under army rule since last November following a disputed election.
What will the referendum decide?
Guinea-Bissau's junta has unanimously approved a constitutional amendment to switch the country from what it frames as a parliamentary to a presidential system.
This means abandoning the old system where the prime minister came from the parliamentary majority.
The amendment would allow the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and dissolve parliament.
If passed, the new constitution will cut the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65.
The junta says the change seeks to stabilize institutions before new presidential and parliamentary elections, scheduled for December 6, which are meant to hand power back to civilians.
Opposition groups, however, have urged the public to boycott the vote, saying it will allow the junta leader to cement power and calling it a "source of political instability at all levels."
When are the results due?
Polls close at 1700 GMT on Sunday, with the first provisional results due from Tuesday.
One of the world's poorest countries, Guinea-Bissau has experienced five coups and a series of attempted coups since 1974.
A military government seized power in November following a disputed election in which former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory.
After legislative elections in 2023, Embalo himself dissolved the opposition-dominated parliament in response to what he described as an attempted coup.

Iran shines at International Earth Science Olympiad
TEHRAN – Iranian students concluded their participation in the 19th International Earth Science Olympiad (IESO 2026) in Italy with an impressive haul of two silver medals, six bronze medals and a top prize.
Mehraneh Vashaqani-Farahani secured the world’s top ranking in the Young Reporters of the International Union of Geological Sciences short documentary category, delivering one of the most notable results for the Iranian team at this year’s competition, IRNA reported.
In the individual examinations, Shamim Molla-Qolizadeh and Javad Namjoo each won a silver medal, while Ghazal Qazizadeh took bronze.
Namjoo also won a bronze medal in the Earth System Project (ESP) category. In the International Team Field Investigation (ITFI), Molla-Qolizadeh, Namjoo, Qazizadeh and Vashaqani-Farahani each earned a bronze medal.
Overall, Iranian representatives won eight medals across the individual and team events at this year’s International Earth Science Olympiad, comprising two silver and six bronze medals. Iran also secured the world’s top ranking in the short documentary category.
The IESO 2026 was held from August 20 to 27 in Turin, Italy. More than 160 students from 41 countries took part in the international scientific competition.
The International Earth Science Olympiad is regarded as one of the major international academic competitions for school students in the fields of Earth sciences, geology and environmental science. Participants compete in theoretical examinations, field activities and international team projects.
IESO is an educational event for secondary school students, not 9lder than 18, globally, organized by the International Geoscience Education Organization (IGEO).
Its aim is to enhance the level of geoscience education worldwide and increase public awareness of Earth Sciences.
It is one of the twelve International Science Olympiads. The first IESO was held in Daegu, South Korea, in 2007, and it has been held annually since, attracting over 200 students from more than 40 countries and regions each year.
Most recently, Iranian students succeeded to win a bronze medal and three honorable mentions at the 22nd International Geography Olympiad (iGeo) held from August 11 to 17 in Istanbul, Turkey.
The International Geography Olympiad is the world’s premier academic competition for secondary school students. It is held under the auspices of the International Geographical Union (IGU) and organized by the IGU Olympiad Commission. This year’s competition brought together more than 180 participants from over 50 countries.
Helia Khodabandelou grabbed the bronze medal, while Setayesh Haqnazari, Artina Heidari, and Sana Karbalaei received international diploma of honors.

articles.title: Dining across the divide: ‘He says he feels pride about being English, but I don’t’
articles.body:
Finley, 23, London
Occupation Planetary scientist
Voting record Labour before the last election, where he voted Green, and will stick to Green “if Andy Burnham goes ahead with North Sea oil drilling”
Amuse bouche During university, he worked on a project with Nasa on Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons. He loved it so much he got a tattoo of Europa on his right shoulder
Gavin, 54, London
Occupation Retired software engineer
Voting record Tory “out of habit and upbringing” until Brexit; ever since then, Lib Dem and sometimes Green
Amuse bouche He and his wife went on holiday to Australia in 2003 and met the actor Rob Lowe at their hotel, but had never seen him in anything so didn’t recognise him. When they later asked for a photo, his “jokey condition” was that they watch The West Wing when they got home
For starters
Gavin We got on very well. I wouldn’t normally go to a vegan restaurant, but my daughter is vegan and I’ve told her she should go there.
Finley It was extremely enjoyable – my nerves melted away quickly. The food was fantastic, and Gavin and I got along better than I expected.
Gavin I started with roti with three sauces. Then I had chickpea curry with greens, and a beer. It was all very nice.
Finley I started with amazing deep-fried dumplings. Then I had plant-based fish with coconut, lentils and braised tomatoes, and some pineapple and kimchi pholourie, which were almost like pakoras. Fantastic.
The big beef
Gavin I don’t think the state should try to compete with the open market; the open market is always going to be cheaper, as they will always try to reduce costs.
Finley If you give power to the state to control, for example, utility companies, the service will be provided for the constituents’ benefit, not the shareholders’ benefit.
Gavin We did talk about Thames Water. I think in the case of utilities, state-run companies actually could do a better job than the free market – but they will also be somewhat hamstrung by unions.
Finley We talked about how privatisation essentially ruined a lot of utility companies, because there was no motivation for the shareholders to provide a good service. They just want profits, which is why the CEOs at water companies have been reporting record-high wages as the service worsens.
Sharing plate
Gavin I would be in favour of legalising drugs. The tax could provide another revenue stream for the government – plus, it takes away the incentive for crime. I think people should be allowed to do whatever they want as long as they don’t hurt anyone else.
Finley I think if we decriminalise drugs and treat addiction like a healthcare problem, the symptoms suffered by wider society will also be treated – as we’ve seen in Portugal. Instead of spending millions on drug policing, spend it on rehabilitation and healthcare programmes that will target the issue in a more humane manner.
For afters
Gavin I don’t find flags hung from lamp-posts intimidating – a lot of flags give a positive message, such as the Ukraine flag when the war started, LGBTQ flags – but context matters. During the World Cup, when I saw St George’s flags, I’m annoyed that I had to stop and think: “Wait, what does that mean?” because the England flag has been purloined by the far right.
Finley When you’re putting flags in a public place where communities are diverse, it has the connotation of division. Gavin says he feels some pride about being English, but I don’t. There seems to be something about Englishness that’s violent and divisive. I don’t really want to see the English flag wherever I go – even during the World Cup, knowing domestic abuse rates go up when England lose.
Takeaways
Gavin Finley gave me hope. I think part of the problem with politics is it pushes people into pigeonholes: left wing or right wing. And actually, if you have a proper conversation, you realise everyone wants broadly the same thing.
Finley I think people from older generations need to be more optimistic. If we lean in to cynicism, nothing will get done. But Gavin was also really climate positive, and that was so refreshing to hear. I think this type of conversation should be had more often, and food is a fantastic way to facilitate that.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.
Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.

Ukrainian canoeist wins World Championship gold in C-1 200 metres
Ukrainian canoeist Liudmyla Luzan has won a gold medal at the 2026 ICF Canoe Sprint World Championships in Poznań, Poland.
Source: Champion, a sports news platform within Ukrainska Pravda's holding company
Details: On the final competition day of the world championships, three-time Olympic medallist Luzan triumphed in the C-1 200 metres final.
Luzan finished first with a time of 44.40 seconds, beating her nearest rival – Canadian Sophia Jensen – by 0.50 seconds.
The 29-year-old Ukrainian athlete has thus defended her world championship title in this discipline. She triumphed at the world championships in Milan last year.
This is Luzan's second medal at the 2026 world championships in Poznań. She previously won a silver medal together with Anastasiia Rybachok in the C-2 500 metres.

articles.title: Ferry carrying more than 250 passengers capsizes off northern Cyprus
articles.body:
Rescue under way after ferry with more than 260 on board capsizes off northern Cyprus
At least six people died when a ferry carrying more than 260 people capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, the head of the local government said, offering a preliminary toll to Turkish media. Rescue crews were dispatched to the scene, with footage showing passengers in life jackets in the water around the overturned vessel.
The catamaran-style ferry was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
At least six people have died in the disaster, Turkish media reported. Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), said the vessel had been carrying a total of 267 people when it rolled over shortly after leaving port, according to Turkish state news agency Anadolu.
Ustel added that 172 people had so far been rescued and that operations were continuing to evacuate the remaining passengers and crew, Anadolu said
The privately owned ferry left the North Cyprus port of Kyrenia at 12.30pm local time (0930 GMT) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, Anadolu reported.

The ferry started taking in water a few kilometres (miles) off the coast, the Turkish state-run TRT news channel reported.
Northern Cyprus Transportation Minister Erhan Arikli told TRT that the ship had overturned and that rescue crews were already on the scene.
Several companies run ferries on the busy route between Kyrenia and Tasucu. It is not yet known which company was operating the ferry that capsized.
Video footage from the scene shows people with life-vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.
Erdogan set to visit northern Cyprus
The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkey, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.
Ankara occupied that part of the island that year in response to an Athens-engineered Greek Cypriot coup seeking union with Greece. The TRNC today is served with regular air and sea links to Turkey.
"All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's health ministry said in a statement.
It added that hospitals in the territory had been alerted, so they could provide any medical attention that might be needed.
The TRNC is dependent on Turkey, and Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on X that "we are providing all necessary assistance to the search and rescue operations".
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is scheduled to visit the TRNC on Monday to see its president, Tufan Erhurmann, who was elected by the territory's voters in October.
The visit would be Erdogan's first since 2023.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: How to make key lime pie | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
articles.body:
Beautiful as the Florida Keys are, with average August temperatures topping 30C and with hurricane season looming, I think I’d rather enjoy their most famous culinary export in the calm of our own more temperate isles (well, usually, at least). Cool and creamy, with a refreshingly sharp, citrus tang, this is the perfect make-ahead dessert for any bank holiday festivities.
Prep 20 min
 Cook 15 min
 Chill 3 hr+
 Serves 6
For the base
75g butter, or coconut oil, plus extra for greasing
200g digestive biscuits (about 13)
1 pinch salt
For the filling
4-5 limes
  4 egg yolks
400g tin condensed milk
For the topping (optional – see steps 8 and 9)
300ml whipping or double cream
  1 tbsp icing sugar
1 A note on the biscuits
In the States, this would involve graham crackers, which are sweeter and more crisp than our digestive biscuits. The latter do make a decent substitute, but feel free to swap in any other biscuits you like the idea of with lime (I suspect ginger nuts would be rather good).
2 Start on the pie crust
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and lightly grease a 20cm tart tin – not too shallow a one, ideally, and preferably loose-bottomed if you’re planning on taking the pie out of the tin to serve. Crush the biscuits to a fine crumb, either using a food processor or by wrapping them in a clean tea towel and whacking with a rolling pin.
3 Pack the crust into the tin
Melt the fat in a microwave or a small saucepan – butter is the classic choice, but I like the flavour of coconut oil here – then stir into the crumbs with a pinch of salt. Tip into the tin, use your hands to press down the mix into an even crust across the base and up the sides, then press down again with the base of a glass.
4 Bake, then cool
Bake the crust for about 15 minutes, until it’s dry to the touch, then take out of the oven and leave to cool (though not mandatory, this step will give a crisper crust that holds together much better upon slicing, so it’s worth turning on the oven for).
5 Wash and zest the limes
Key limes are a distinct variety of thin-skinned, aromatic citrus that are hard to get outside the Americas. Happily, though not an exact match, this recipe works just as well with standard limes, especially if you use the zest as well as the juice. Scrub the fruit under hot water, then finely grate the zest into a large bowl.
6 Juice the limes
Squeeze the juice from the zested limes into a jug until you have about 120ml, straining out any pips as you go. Add the egg yolks to the zest bowl (the whites make a lovely meringue topping, if you’re looking for a way to use them up: see step 9 for a suggested recipe to replace the cream).
7 Beat the egg yolks and zest
Beat the yolks and zest for a couple of minutes with a whisk, electric beaters or a food mixer until the mixture thickens and turns pale green, then stir in the condensed milk. Beat in the lime juice – the mix should be shockingly tangy and sweet; chilling will mute the lime flavour, so add more juice, if you like – then pour the filling into the cooled biscuit shell.
8 Chill, then top with cream
Chill for at least three hours, until set. If you’re planning on topping your pie with cream, whisk this and the sugar in a large bowl until the mix holds soft peaks, then dollop on top of the set filling. Garnish with extra slices of lime, if you have them, or some grated lime zest, and serve.
9 … or top with meringue
If you prefer a meringue topping (and to use up some excess egg whites into the bargain) – for the sweet toothed only! – whisk two of the egg whites to soft peaks, then beat in 115g sugar a tablespoon at a time, until the mix is glossy and holds its shape. Beat in half a teaspoon of vinegar or lime/lemon juice, then spoon on top the pie. Brown briefly with a blowtorch or under a hot grill before serving.

Ferry carrying over 260 people capsizes off Cyprus
August 30, 2026
A passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, shortly after leaving port, the local government said.
Six people have died, Turkish state media reported, citing Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC).
Ustel said that around 100 passengers had been evacuated.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974, with the northern part under the administration of the TRNC, which is recognized internationally only by Turkey.
Passenger boat heading from northern Cyprus to Turkey
Turkish media reported that a ferry carrying more than 260 passengers was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in southern Mersin province, when it sank.
Erhan Arikli, the TRNC's Transport Minister, told Turkish and Cypriot media that there were 267 people on board — 259 passengers and 8 crew members.
"All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's Health Ministry said in a statement.
Search and rescue operations ongoing
In a post on X, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said: "We are closely following the unfortunate incident that has occurred and providing all possible support to the search and rescue efforts."
Turkey's state-run TRT news channel reported that the ferry began taking on water 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) from the coast.

articles.title: EU needs Russia as ‘external enemy’ to collect more taxes — Kremlin
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. European authorities are trying to portray Russia as an "external enemy" in order to collect more taxes from their populations for their defense capabilities, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalist Pavel Zarubin.
"Having lost their very cheap American security umbrella, Europeans are now building their own defense identity. This costs a great deal of money. To do so, they must take their taxpayers out of their comfort zones by forcing them to pay significantly more in higher rent, taxes, electricity, and gasoline," he explained.
The spokesman noted that voters do not like this. "How do you convince voters? By inventing an enemy. What kind of enemy is most convincing? A big one, a large, powerful one," Peskov emphasized.
